modules.title: Vikkypaedia Medicine Basics (Harrison's 22nd Edition)
modules.subtitle: 10 Core Units · 30 Extracted Harrison's 22e Chapters · 3-Tier CBME Mastery (L1 Nurse, L2 MBBS, L3 PG)
learningObjectives: Apply dual-process reasoning, Bayes' theorem (Post-test odds = Pre-test odds × LR), and cognitive debiasing to reduce diagnostic errors (Ch. 1, 4, 10).
Integrate high-LR bedside physical examination signs, Wilson-Jungner screening principles, and Swiss Cheese patient safety into daily ward practice (Ch. 2, 6, 7, 8).
Distinguish PGE2-mediated fever (>37.7°C) from hyperthermia, manage febrile petechial shock immediately, and structure an FUO workup (Ch. 20, 21, 22).
Execute the 10-minute lethal chest discomfort exclusion protocol and differentiate visceral, parietal, and extra-abdominal pain mimics (Ch. 14, 15, 16).
Classify hypoxemia using the A–a O2 gradient, recognize the severe anemia cyanosis trap (>4 g/dL deoxyHb), and localize edema via Starling forces & JVP (Ch. 39, 42, 43).
Stratify cardiac vs reflex/orthostatic syncope, manage hypoactive delirium non-pharmacologically, and run the 5-minute emergency coma sequence (Ch. 23, 29, 30).
Apply restrictive transfusion (<7 g/dL) in acute GI bleeding, branch conjugated vs unconjugated jaundice, and interpret SAAG & ascitic PMN >=250/uL for SBP (Ch. 51, 52, 53).
Prevent Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (<=8–10 mEq/L/24h), execute the hyperkalemia emergency triad, and solve mixed ABGs via Winter's equation & albumin-corrected AG (Ch. 56, 58).
Differentiate prerenal vs ATN vs postrenal AKI, interpret RPI & MCV anemia workups, and decode primary vs secondary hemostasis & mixing studies (Ch. 55, 66, 69).
Prescribe safely using Vd-based loading doses, clearance-based maintenance doses, decision-making capacity criteria, and SPIKES palliative communication (Ch. 71, 12, 13).

units.title: The Practice of Medicine, Clinical Reasoning & Diagnostic Safety
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 1, 4 & 10 — Dual-Process Reasoning, Bayes' Theorem & Reducing Diagnostic Errors

points.title: The Enduring Clinical Triad of Internal Medicine [Ref 1]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 (The Editors) [Ref 1]:** Effective clinical care rests on three inseparable pillars: **scientific knowledge**, **technical bedside skill**, and **human understanding**. A patient is never a collection of lab values or imaging reports—history taking alone establishes the working diagnosis in ~70–80% of medical encounters.

points.title: Dual-Process Clinical Reasoning: System 1 vs System 2 [Ref 3]
rows: Rapid triage in classic emergencies (STEMI, anaphylaxis)

points.title: The 3 Mandatory Diagnostic Time-Out Questions [Ref 7, 35]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 10 (Schiff) [Ref 7]** and the **National Academy of Medicine [Ref 35]**, clinicians prevent missed diagnoses by pausing to ask: **(1)** What else could this be? **(2)** Is anything inconsistent with my working diagnosis? **(3)** **What critical diagnoses can I NOT afford to miss?**

quiz.text: According to Harrison's 22nd Edition Ch. 1, which clinical activity remains the single most powerful contributor to establishing an accurate initial diagnosis?
quiz.stem: According to Harrison's 22nd Edition Ch. 1, which clinical activity remains the single most powerful contributor to establishing an accurate initial diagnosis?
options: Whole-body CT scanning prior to seeing the patient
A thorough, empathetic patient history integrated with focused physical examination
Ordering a 40-panel broad biochemical screen on every clinic visit
Relying exclusively on automated electronic health record problem lists
hints: Think about what happens before any lab test is ordered.
Clinical diagnosis begins with listening to the patient's narrative and observing bedside signs.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 emphasizes history and physical examination as the foundational core of medical diagnosis.
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 [Ref 1] underscores that careful history-taking paired with a purposeful physical examination generates the primary diagnostic hypotheses and guides rational, cost-effective testing.

quiz.text: Which cognitive error occurs when a clinician locks onto the first plausible diagnosis (e.g., 'viral gastroenteritis') and stops considering alternatives despite worsening abdominal pain?
quiz.stem: Which cognitive error occurs when a clinician locks onto the first plausible diagnosis (e.g., 'viral gastroenteritis') and stops considering alternatives despite worsening abdominal pain?
options: Premature closure
Lead-time bias
Regression to the mean
Spectrum bias
hints: Think about closing the diagnostic door too early.
The clinician failed to ask 'What else could this be?' once an initial label felt comfortable.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 10 identifies premature closure as the single most common cognitive driver of diagnostic error.
quiz.rationale: Premature closure—accepting a diagnosis before full verification and failing to entertain alternatives—is the leading cognitive bias causing missed and delayed diagnoses [Ref 7].

quiz.text: A clinic nurse notices a patient's hemoglobin dropped from 13.0 to 9.2 g/dL, but the abnormal lab report was never communicated to the physician or patient. What system safeguard from Ch. 10 prevents this failure?
quiz.stem: A clinic nurse notices a patient's hemoglobin dropped from 13.0 to 9.2 g/dL, but the abnormal lab report was never communicated to the physician or patient. What system safeguard from Ch. 10 prevents this failure?
options: Banning nurses from viewing lab results
Closed-loop test result tracking and team-based diagnostic communication
Repeating the CBC only if the patient returns next year
Relying on patients to remember to call the lab
hints: How do we guarantee critical test results never fall through the cracks?
The National Academy of Medicine emphasizes active tracking and team empowerment.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 10 & NAM Table 10-1 highlight closed-loop follow-up and interprofessional teamwork.
quiz.rationale: Closed-loop test result tracking and empowering nurses, patients, and clinicians as a diagnostic team directly prevent missed critical results [Ref 7, 35].

quiz.text: What is the primary purpose of taking a brief 'diagnostic time-out' before discharging a patient with unexplained symptoms?
quiz.stem: What is the primary purpose of taking a brief 'diagnostic time-out' before discharging a patient with unexplained symptoms?
options: To bill additional hospital hours
To explicitly ask 'What critical diagnoses can I not afford to miss?' and test against disconfirming evidence
To delay urgent resuscitation
To replace the physical examination
hints: Why pause System 1 autopilot?
Deliberate reflection engages System 2 to catch high-risk 'don't-miss' mimics.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 10 explicitly prescribes asking what critical diagnoses must not be missed.
quiz.rationale: A diagnostic time-out engages analytical System 2 thinking to test for disconfirming findings and rule out lethal 'don't-miss' conditions before finalizing disposition [Ref 7].

quiz.text: In clinical decision-making (Harrison's 22e Ch. 4), how does Bayes' theorem update disease probability after a diagnostic test?
quiz.stem: In clinical decision-making (Harrison's 22e Ch. 4), how does Bayes' theorem update disease probability after a diagnostic test?
options: Post-test Probability = Pre-test Probability × Sensitivity
Post-test Odds = Pre-test Odds × Likelihood Ratio (LR)
Post-test Odds = Specificity / Prevalence
Post-test Probability is independent of Pre-test Probability
hints: Remember that Bayes' theorem works cleanly in ODDS space, not raw percentages.
Convert probability P to odds P/(1-P), then multiply by LR+ or LR−.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 4 states: Post-test Odds = Pre-test Odds × LR.
quiz.rationale: Bayes' theorem in odds form states: Post-test Odds = Pre-test Odds × Likelihood Ratio, where LR+ = Sensitivity / (1 − Specificity) and LR− = (1 − Sensitivity) / Specificity [Ref 3].

quiz.text: A D-dimer test has a sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 45% for pulmonary embolism. What is its approximate Negative Likelihood Ratio (LR−), and what does a negative result mean in a low-risk patient?
quiz.stem: A D-dimer test has a sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 45% for pulmonary embolism. What is its approximate Negative Likelihood Ratio (LR−), and what does a negative result mean in a low-risk patient?
options: LR− ≈ 0.09 — strongly rules OUT pulmonary embolism (SnNout)
LR− ≈ 10.5 — strongly rules IN pulmonary embolism
LR− ≈ 1.0 — provides zero diagnostic value
LR− ≈ 2.2 — moderately increases PE probability
hints: Recall the formula for LR−: (1 − Sensitivity) / Specificity.
Plug in Sensitivity = 0.96 and Specificity = 0.45: 0.04 / 0.45 ≈ 0.09.
An LR− < 0.1 produces a large shift downward in post-test probability [Ch. 4].
quiz.rationale: LR− = (1 − 0.96) / 0.45 = 0.089 (<0.1), generating a large reduction in post-test probability that safely rules out PE when pre-test probability is low [Ref 3].

quiz.text: Why does ordering a test with 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity in a population where disease prevalence is only 1% result in MOST positive tests being false positives?
quiz.stem: Why does ordering a test with 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity in a population where disease prevalence is only 1% result in MOST positive tests being false positives?
options: Because sensitivity drops to 1% in healthy people
Because Positive Predictive Value (PPV) depends heavily on pre-test prevalence: true positives (0.95%) are outnumbered by false positives (4.95%)
Because specificity only applies to hospitalized patients
Because LR+ equals zero when prevalence is low
hints: Imagine testing 1,000 people with 1% prevalence (10 sick, 990 healthy).
Of 10 sick, ~9.5 test positive. Of 990 healthy, 5% (~50) test falsely positive!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 4 warns against 'shotgun' testing in very low pre-test probability populations.
quiz.rationale: In 1,000 patients at 1% prevalence, 9.5 are true positives vs ~50 false positives (PPV ≈ 16%). Low pre-test probability makes indiscriminate testing a source of false-positive cascades [Ref 3].

quiz.text: When a clinician estimates a patient's pre-test probability of bacterial pneumonia is ALREADY above the 'treatment threshold' (e.g., 85%), what is the optimal Bayesian management step?
quiz.stem: When a clinician estimates a patient's pre-test probability of bacterial pneumonia is ALREADY above the 'treatment threshold' (e.g., 85%), what is the optimal Bayesian management step?
options: Order three additional low-LR tests to reach 100% certainty before starting antibiotics
Initiate empiric treatment directly, because no further test result would drop probability below the treatment threshold
Withhold therapy until culture results return in 72 hours
Ignore the physical exam and discharge the patient
hints: Think about the test-treatment threshold model in Harrison's Ch. 4.
Testing is only valuable when its result can cross either the testing or treatment threshold.
Above the treatment threshold, testing adds cost/delay without changing management [Ref 3].
quiz.rationale: Per Harrison's 22e Ch. 4 threshold analysis [Ref 3], diagnostic tests should only be ordered when pre-test probability lies in the intermediate zone between the 'test threshold' and 'treatment threshold'.

quiz.text: A physician just treated two patients with aortic dissection this week and now orders urgent CT angiography on a healthy 22-year-old with reproducible chest wall tenderness after push-ups. Which specific heuristic bias is operating?
quiz.stem: A physician just treated two patients with aortic dissection this week and now orders urgent CT angiography on a healthy 22-year-old with reproducible chest wall tenderness after push-ups. Which specific heuristic bias is operating?
options: Availability bias
Omission bias
Spectrum bias
Verification bias
hints: Recent, vivid, or emotionally memorable cases come to mind too easily.
Judging probability by how easily an example is recalled is a classic Tversky-Kahneman heuristic.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 4 & 10 define this as availability bias.
quiz.rationale: Availability bias occurs when recent or dramatic clinical encounters distort a clinician's estimate of pre-test probability for subsequent patients [Ref 3, 7].

quiz.text: On a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve comparing two diagnostic biomarkers, what does an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.50 indicate?
quiz.stem: On a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve comparing two diagnostic biomarkers, what does an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.50 indicate?
options: Perfect diagnostic discrimination
Discrimination no better than a random coin flip
100% sensitivity with 50% specificity
Optimal test threshold for rule-out
hints: An ROC curve plots Sensitivity (y-axis) against 1 − Specificity (x-axis).
The diagonal line from (0,0) to (1,1) has area 0.50.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 4 notes AUC = 1.0 is perfect and AUC = 0.50 is chance alone.
quiz.rationale: An ROC AUC of 0.50 represents the line of identity (Sensitivity = 1 − Specificity), meaning the test provides no discriminatory information beyond random chance [Ref 3].

quiz.text: Why does Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 caution against indiscriminate 'shotgun' laboratory testing?
quiz.stem: Why does Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 caution against indiscriminate 'shotgun' laboratory testing?
options: Labs are always completely inaccurate
Broad unguided testing increases false-positive cascades, patient harm, anxiety, and healthcare costs without improving diagnostic accuracy
Physicians are not permitted to order lab panels
Only CT scans produce false positives
hints: Think about what happens when you run 40 tests on a healthy patient (5% abnormal by chance each).
Unnecessary incidentalomas trigger invasive downstream procedures.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 champions hypothesis-driven diagnostic stewardship [Ref 1].
quiz.rationale: Unguided shotgun testing generates inevitable false positives and incidentalomas that cascade into harmful procedures and wasted resources; testing must be guided by clinical hypotheses [Ref 1].

quiz.text: How does Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 define the optimal relationship between clinical expertise and Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM)?
quiz.stem: How does Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 define the optimal relationship between clinical expertise and Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM)?
options: EBM replaces clinical judgment with rigid algorithms
Integrating the best available external research evidence with individual clinical expertise AND the patient's unique values/preferences
Ignoring clinical trials in favor of personal anecdotes
Using only meta-analyses from before 1990
hints: Think of Sackett's classic three-circle EBM triad cited in Ch. 1.
Research evidence alone cannot decide care without clinical context and patient values.
Evidence + Clinical Expertise + Patient Values = true EBM [Ref 1].
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 1 [Ref 1] frames Evidence-Based Medicine as the triad of best external evidence, bedside clinical judgment, and individual patient values/circumstances.

points.title: Quantitative Test Performance & Likelihood Ratios [Ref 3]
rows: High sensitivity -> Negative test rules OUT (SnNout)
High specificity -> Positive test rules IN (SpPin)
LR+ > 10 produces large, often conclusive increase in probability
LR− < 0.1 produces large, often conclusive decrease in probability

points.title: Pre-Test Probability Anchors Every Lab Order [Ref 3]
points.body: Unlike Sensitivity and Specificity (intrinsic test properties), **Positive and Negative Predictive Values (PPV/NPV)** vary dramatically with disease prevalence. Ordering low-specificity tests in low-prevalence patients triggers harmful diagnostic cascades of incidentalomas and unnecessary invasive procedures.

points.title: Calibration, Threshold Models & Cognitive Forcing Functions [Ref 3, 7]
points.body: Expert diagnosticians integrate **test-treatment thresholds** (weighing harm of missed disease against harm of false-positive treatment) with **cognitive debiasing**: explicitly generating a 3-item differential, actively searching for disconfirming cues, and reviewing longitudinal clinical trajectories when patients fail to improve as expected.

units.title: The Physical Examination, Prevention, Screening & Patient Safety
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 2, 6, 7 & 8 — High-LR Bedside Signs, Screening Biases & Swiss Cheese Safety

points.title: Why the Physical Examination Still Saves Lives [Ref 6]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 8 (Verghese & McGee) [Ref 6]:** Over-reliance on computer screens creates the **'iPatient'** phenomenon while missing high-value bedside diagnoses that imaging cannot replace: **herpes zoster rash**, **asymmetric arm BP in aortic dissection**, **elevated JVP**, **pulsus paradoxus**, **asterixis**, and **silent hyperthyroidism/Parkinsonism**.

points.title: Patient Safety: Reason's Swiss Cheese Model [Ref 5]
points.body: In **Harrison's 22e Ch. 7 (Bates) [Ref 5]**, adverse events rarely stem from a single 'bad' clinician; they occur when **active failures** (slips at the sharp end) align with **latent system conditions** (poor handoffs, look-alike vials, alarm fatigue, understaffing). Building a **Just Culture** replaces blame with system redesign, checklists, and standardized handoffs (e.g., I-PASS).

points.title: Primordial vs Primary vs Secondary vs Tertiary Prevention [Ref 2, 4]
rows: Prevent emergence of risk factors themselves
Smoke-free public policy, healthy urban food environments
Prevent disease onset in susceptible individuals
Vaccination (HPV, influenza, pneumococcal), statins before MI
Colonoscopy, mammography, cervical cytology, BP & HIV screening
ACEi in diabetic nephropathy, cardiac rehab post-MI

quiz.text: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 8 (Verghese & McGee), what does the term 'iPatient' warn clinicians against?
quiz.stem: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 8 (Verghese & McGee), what does the term 'iPatient' warn clinicians against?
options: Using smartphones for clinical calculators
Focusing predominantly on the electronic chart, labs, and scans while neglecting direct bedside physical examination of the real patient
Allowing patients to read their own medical records
Using point-of-care ultrasound at the bedside
hints: Think about what happens when doctors spend more time looking at monitors than touching patients.
Verghese coined 'iPatient' for the digital avatar in the EHR.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 8 stresses that bedside examination both uncovers vital signs and builds therapeutic trust.
quiz.rationale: Verghese and McGee [Ref 6] warn that treating the digital 'iPatient' in the EHR leads to missed bedside diagnoses (rashes, JVP, murmurs, neurologic signs) and erosion of the healing doctor-patient bond.

quiz.text: In Reason's Swiss Cheese Model of healthcare safety (Harrison's 22e Ch. 7), when does a patient harm event occur?
quiz.stem: In Reason's Swiss Cheese Model of healthcare safety (Harrison's 22e Ch. 7), when does a patient harm event occur?
options: Only when a clinician intentionally violates hospital policy
When holes in successive system defenses (active failures + latent conditions) align, allowing a hazard to reach the patient
Whenever an electronic medical record is upgraded
Only in surgical operating rooms
hints: Visualize slices of Swiss cheese representing layers of safety barriers.
Adverse events happen when the holes line up across every layer.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 7 contrasts sharp-end active failures with blunt-end latent pathogens.
quiz.rationale: Reason's Swiss Cheese Model [Ref 5] demonstrates that serious medical errors arise when latent system vulnerabilities (fatigue, look-alike packaging, poor handoffs) align with an active human slip.

quiz.text: Which intervention is an example of SECONDARY prevention according to Harrison's 22e Ch. 6?
quiz.stem: Which intervention is an example of SECONDARY prevention according to Harrison's 22e Ch. 6?
options: Administering Hepatitis B vaccine to a healthcare worker
Performing routine colonoscopy in an asymptomatic 50-year-old adult to detect early polyps/colorectal cancer
Prescribing beta-blockers after an acute myocardial infarction
Enacting clean-air legislation to prevent smoking initiation
hints: Primary prevents disease before it starts; Secondary detects asymptomatic latent disease.
Screening asymptomatic individuals for precancerous polyps or early cancer is Secondary prevention.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 6 defines screening as the cornerstone of secondary prevention.
quiz.rationale: Secondary prevention detects asymptomatic disease in a latent stage where early intervention improves outcomes (e.g., colorectal cancer screening, cervical Pap/HPV testing, BP screening) [Ref 4].

quiz.text: Which hospital safety practice directly reduces medication errors and communication breakdowns during shift changes?
quiz.stem: Which hospital safety practice directly reduces medication errors and communication breakdowns during shift changes?
options: Verbal-only hallway sign-outs without written summaries
Standardized structured handoffs (e.g., I-PASS), medication reconciliation, and computerized order safety checks
Punishing nurses who report near-miss events
Eliminating checklists to save time
hints: Think about what prevents lost critical tasks between day and night shifts.
Harrison's Ch. 7 emphasizes standardized handoffs, CPOE, and non-punitive near-miss reporting.
Just Culture encourages near-miss reporting so latent flaws are fixed before harm occurs.
quiz.rationale: Standardized handoffs, medication reconciliation, CPOE clinical decision support, and a non-punitive reporting culture measurably cut preventable adverse drug events [Ref 5].

quiz.text: What is 'Lead-Time Bias' when evaluating a new cancer screening test (Harrison's 22e Ch. 6)?
quiz.stem: What is 'Lead-Time Bias' when evaluating a new cancer screening test (Harrison's 22e Ch. 6)?
options: Screening detects faster-growing tumors earlier than slower ones
Earlier detection moves the diagnosis date backward, making post-diagnosis survival APPEAR longer even though the actual date of death is unchanged
Only wealthy patients volunteer for screening
A screening test has low specificity
hints: Imagine a patient destined to die at age 70: diagnosed at 68 = 2y survival; screened at 63 = 7y survival — did they live longer?
No! Only the 'lead time' between diagnosis and death increased.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 6 stresses that true screening efficacy requires reduced disease-specific MORTALITY, not just longer survival time.
quiz.rationale: Lead-time bias artificially inflates 5-year survival statistics simply by starting the clock earlier without delaying death; valid screening trials must demonstrate reduced mortality [Ref 4].

quiz.text: What is 'Length-Time Bias' in disease screening programs?
quiz.stem: What is 'Length-Time Bias' in disease screening programs?
options: Screening preferentially detects slow-growing, indolent cancers with a long preclinical phase while missing rapidly aggressive interval cancers
Screening tests take too long to process in rural clinics
Patients forget how long they have had symptoms
Screening lengthens hospital stay
hints: Picture casting a net periodically: slow-moving fish spend longer in the window and are more likely to be caught.
Slow-growing tumors naturally have better prognosis regardless of screening.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 6 explains length-time bias and overdiagnosis as key traps in observational screening data.
quiz.rationale: Length-time bias occurs because periodic screening disproportionately captures indolent tumors with long asymptomatic phases, overestimating screening benefit unless evaluated by RCT mortality [Ref 4].

quiz.text: Which high-yield bedside physical examination sign has strong evidence (high LR+) for elevated left ventricular filling pressures / heart failure?
quiz.stem: Which high-yield bedside physical examination sign has strong evidence (high LR+) for elevated left ventricular filling pressures / heart failure?
options: Isolated 1+ bilateral ankle edema in a patient on amlodipine
Elevated Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP >8 cm H2O) and a third heart sound (S3 gallop)
Normal vesicular breath sounds
Mild sinus tachycardia at 102 bpm
hints: Think of the classic high-LR cardiovascular exam findings in Harrison's Ch. 8.
Elevated JVP reflects right atrial pressure and tracks LV filling pressure; S3 reflects rapid early diastolic filling into a stiff/dilated ventricle.
Both JVP elevation and S3 gallop carry high positive likelihood ratios for decompensated heart failure.
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 8 [Ref 6] highlights elevated JVP and an S3 gallop (along with positive hepatojugular reflux) as high-LR bedside indicators of elevated filling pressures and heart failure.

quiz.text: According to Wilson-Jungner criteria (Harrison's 22e Ch. 6 Table 6-1), why is routine population screening for a rare, rapidly fatal malignancy with NO effective early treatment inappropriate?
quiz.stem: According to Wilson-Jungner criteria (Harrison's 22e Ch. 6 Table 6-1), why is routine population screening for a rare, rapidly fatal malignancy with NO effective early treatment inappropriate?
options: Because screening violates the requirement for a detectable latent stage AND an effective early intervention that improves outcomes
Because screening tests are always painful
Because primary care physicians cannot order imaging
Because specificity is always 100%
hints: Review Table 6-1 'Principles of Screening' from Harrison's 22e Ch. 6.
Without effective early treatment, screening only creates anxiety, overdiagnosis, and procedural harm.
Effective screening requires an important health problem, a latent stage, an accurate acceptable test, and effective early therapy.
quiz.rationale: Per Harrison's 22e Ch. 6 Table 6-1 [Ref 4], screening is only justified when early detection during a latent phase enables effective intervention that reduces morbidity or mortality.

quiz.text: If a screening intervention reduces 10-year disease-specific mortality from 0.8% (unscreened) to 0.6% (screened), what is the Number Needed to Screen (NNS) to prevent 1 death?
quiz.stem: If a screening intervention reduces 10-year disease-specific mortality from 0.8% (unscreened) to 0.6% (screened), what is the Number Needed to Screen (NNS) to prevent 1 death?
hints: First compute the Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR) = 0.8% − 0.6%.
quiz.rationale: Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR) = 0.008 − 0.006 = 0.002; therefore NNS = 1 / 0.002 = 500 individuals screened over 10 years to prevent one death [Ref 4].

quiz.text: In Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 (Lloyd-Jones & McKibbin), what distinguishes 'Primordial Prevention' from 'Primary Prevention'?
quiz.stem: In Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 (Lloyd-Jones & McKibbin), what distinguishes 'Primordial Prevention' from 'Primary Prevention'?
options: Primordial prevention prevents the development of upstream risk factors (e.g., obesity, hypertension, tobacco exposure) across the life course rather than merely treating established risk factors
Primordial prevention uses high-dose statins in every child
Primordial prevention applies only to genetic diseases
Primordial and tertiary prevention are synonyms
hints: Think one step earlier than treating hypertension or hyperlipidemia.
How do we keep ideal cardiovascular health from birth so hypertension never develops?
Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 emphasizes primordial prevention as preserving the 'stock of health' across the lifespan.
quiz.rationale: Primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence of risk factors themselves (through nutrition, physical activity, tobacco avoidance, and equitable environments), whereas primary prevention treats existing risk factors before clinical disease occurs [Ref 2].

quiz.text: Which structured 5-step behavioral counseling framework in Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 helps primary care clinicians double tobacco cessation rates?
quiz.stem: Which structured 5-step behavioral counseling framework in Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 helps primary care clinicians double tobacco cessation rates?
options: The 5 A's: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange
The 5 R's of antibiotic stewardship
The 5 P's of acute limb ischemia
The 5 C's of chest X-ray reading
hints: Every clinical visit should screen for tobacco use and offer structured quit support.
Ask -> Advise -> Assess -> Assist -> Arrange follow-up.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 emphasizes brief structured counseling + pharmacotherapy [Ref 2].
quiz.rationale: The 5 A's framework (Ask, Advise, Assess readiness, Assist with quit plan/pharmacotherapy, Arrange follow-up) significantly increases sustained tobacco cessation [Ref 2].

quiz.text: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 (Promoting Good Health), which category of factors accounts for the LARGEST share of population health outcomes and longevity?
quiz.stem: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 (Promoting Good Health), which category of factors accounts for the LARGEST share of population health outcomes and longevity?
options: Tertiary ICU technology alone
Social determinants of health (income, education, housing, food security, environment) and health behaviors
Annual full-body MRI scans
Genetic sequencing at birth alone
hints: Medical care alone explains only ~10–20% of modifiable population health outcomes!
Where people live, learn, work, and eat shapes disease burden far more than rescue care.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 2 highlights SDOH and primordial prevention [Ref 2].
quiz.rationale: Social determinants of health and behavioral/environmental factors drive the majority of population morbidity and longevity—making primordial prevention and health equity central to medicine [Ref 2].

quiz.text: What is the primary purpose of a non-punitive Root Cause Analysis (RCA) after a serious hospital near-miss or adverse event (Ch. 7)?
quiz.stem: What is the primary purpose of a non-punitive Root Cause Analysis (RCA) after a serious hospital near-miss or adverse event (Ch. 7)?
options: To identify which individual nurse or intern to fire
To uncover latent system flaws (workflow, handoffs, packaging, IT design) and engineer durable safeguards preventing recurrence
To hide the error from hospital leadership
To eliminate medication reconciliation
hints: Remember Reason's Swiss Cheese Model and Just Culture!
Blaming individuals leaves the same broken system trap ready for the next clinician.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 7 uses RCA to fix blunt-end latent system pathogens [Ref 5].
quiz.rationale: Root Cause Analysis investigates how latent system failures allowed an active error to reach the patient, enabling durable system redesign rather than ineffective individual blame [Ref 5].

quiz.text: A patient presents with severe dyspnea and hypotension; systolic BP drops by 18 mmHg during quiet inspiration (Pulsus Paradoxus). Which bedside diagnosis from Ch. 8 must be urgently excluded?
quiz.stem: A patient presents with severe dyspnea and hypotension; systolic BP drops by 18 mmHg during quiet inspiration (Pulsus Paradoxus). Which bedside diagnosis from Ch. 8 must be urgently excluded?
options: Cardiac Tamponade (or severe acute asthma/COPD exacerbation)
Uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia
Benign essential hypertension
Chronic venous insufficiency
hints: Normal inspiratory drop in systolic BP is <10 mmHg.
Exaggerated >12 mmHg inspiratory drop signals ventricular interdependence / impaired filling.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 8 highlights pulsus paradoxus as a high-LR bedside clue to tamponade [Ref 6].
quiz.rationale: Pulsus paradoxus (>10–12 mmHg inspiratory fall in SBP) is a high-value bedside exam sign of cardiac tamponade (or severe obstructive lung disease) requiring immediate bedside POCUS [Ref 6].

points.title: Wilson-Jungner Principles of Effective Screening (Table 6-1) [Ref 4]
points.body: A valid screening program requires: (1) an **important health problem**, (2) a recognizable **latent/asymptomatic stage**, (3) a validated, acceptable screening test, (4) an **effective treatment** where early therapy beats late therapy, and (5) net benefits outweighing harms (false positives, overdiagnosis, radiation/biopsy complications).

points.title: High-Value Bedside Physical Exam Signs & Likelihood Ratios [Ref 6]
rows: High LR+ (5–11) for elevated filling pressures
Strong bedside clue to impaired ventricular filling
Significantly raises pre-test probability before CXR

points.title: Overdiagnosis, Diagnostic Stewardship & POCUS Integration [Ref 4, 5, 6]
points.body: **Overdiagnosis** detects indolent lesions (e.g., subclinical thyroid or prostate microcarcinomas) that would never have caused symptoms or death in the patient's lifetime. Simultaneously, **Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS)** acts as the modern extension of the physical exam—improving bedside accuracy for ascites, pericardial tamponade, pneumothorax, and IVC volume status.

units.title: Approach to Fever, Fever with Rash & Fever of Unknown Origin
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 20, 21 & 22 — Pyrogen Pathophysiology, Petechial Emergencies & FUO Workup

points.title: Harrison's 22nd Edition Definition of Fever vs Hyperthermia [Ref 13]
points.body: **22nd Edition Update (Ch. 20, Dinarello & Surana) [Ref 13]:** Based on large modern thermometry cohorts (mean 36.6°C, 95% CI 35.7–37.3°C), an oral temperature **>37.7°C (>99.9°F, 99th percentile)** defines **fever** (and **>41.5°C** defines **hyperpyrexia**). In **fever**, pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) trigger hypothalamic **PGE2** to RAISE the thermal set-point (responds to antipyretics). In **hyperthermia** (heatstroke, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, serotonin syndrome), the hypothalamic set-point is **UNCHANGED** — **antipyretics DO NOT WORK**; urgent physical cooling and specific antidotes (e.g., dantrolene) are life-saving!

points.title: Fever + Non-Blanching Petechial/Purpuric Rash = Medical Emergency [Ref 14]
rows: Meningococcemia, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, Infective Endocarditis, DIC, Viral Hemorrhagic Fever
Blood cultures + empiric IV antibiotics (Ceftriaxone/Doxycycline) IMMEDIATELY!
Resuscitate shock, stop culprit drugs, clindamycin + vancomycin if TSS
Disseminated Varicella/HSV, Vibrio vulnificus (cirrhosis), Necrotizing Fasciitis
Airborne/contact isolation + IV Acyclovir or emergent surgical debridement

points.title: Sepsis & qSOFA Rapid Rural Bedside Screen [Ref 32]
points.body: Any febrile or hypothermic patient with **>=2 qSOFA points** (**RR >=22**, **altered mentation**, **SBP <=100 mmHg**) requires immediate evaluation for **Sepsis-3** organ dysfunction, blood cultures, **broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour**, balanced crystalloids (**30 mL/kg**), and **Norepinephrine** if MAP remains <65 mmHg.

quiz.text: According to Harrison's 22nd Edition Ch. 20 (Dinarello & Surana), what oral temperature threshold represents the 99th percentile for healthy individuals and defines fever?
quiz.stem: According to Harrison's 22nd Edition Ch. 20 (Dinarello & Surana), what oral temperature threshold represents the 99th percentile for healthy individuals and defines fever?
hints: Recall the updated 22nd edition thermometry benchmark from Ch. 20.
Healthy oral temperatures average ~36.6°C with 95% CI 35.7–37.3°C.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 20 explicitly defines fever as >37.7°C (>99.9°F).
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 20 [Ref 13] defines fever as an oral temperature >37.7°C (>99.9°F), representing the 99th percentile in healthy adults, while >41.5°C defines hyperpyrexia.

quiz.text: A farm worker collapses in 43°C ambient heat with core temperature 41.8°C, hot dry skin, and confusion (exertional/classic heatstroke). Why are oral acetaminophen and ibuprofen INEFFECTIVE here?
quiz.stem: A farm worker collapses in 43°C ambient heat with core temperature 41.8°C, hot dry skin, and confusion (exertional/classic heatstroke). Why are oral acetaminophen and ibuprofen INEFFECTIVE here?
options: Because hyperthermia results from uncontrolled heat production/impaired dissipation with an UNCHANGED hypothalamic set-point — not PGE2-mediated fever
Because NSAIDs raise core body temperature
Because oral drugs cannot dissolve above 40°C
Because heatstroke is caused by interleukin-1
hints: Compare the hypothalamic set-point in fever vs hyperthermia.
Antipyretics inhibit COX -> PGE2 in the hypothalamus to lower an elevated set-point.
In heatstroke, NMS, or malignant hyperthermia, the set-point is already normal — rapid physical cooling is mandatory [Ch. 20].
quiz.rationale: In hyperthermia, the hypothalamic thermal set-point is unchanged; cyclooxygenase inhibitors (acetaminophen/NSAIDs) have zero effect and may worsen hepatic/renal injury. Immediate rapid evaporative/ice-water cooling is required [Ref 13].

quiz.text: A 20-year-old arrives with 39.4°C fever, hypotension (84/50), severe headache, and rapidly spreading non-blanching petechiae on the lower extremities. What is the single highest-priority intervention?
quiz.stem: A 20-year-old arrives with 39.4°C fever, hypotension (84/50), severe headache, and rapidly spreading non-blanching petechiae on the lower extremities. What is the single highest-priority intervention?
options: Schedule a dermatology skin biopsy tomorrow morning
Draw blood cultures and administer empiric IV Ceftriaxone (+ Vancomycin/Dexamethasone) IMMEDIATELY without waiting for CT or LP
Give oral antihistamines for a presumed drug urticaria
Discharge home with oral amoxicillin
hints: Non-blanching petechiae + fever + hypotension = fulminant meningococcemia until proven otherwise!
Every hour of antibiotic delay markedly raises mortality.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 21 mandates immediate empiric IV antimicrobials before imaging or LP.
quiz.rationale: Fever with non-blanching petechiae/purpura and hypotension represents life-threatening meningococcemia (or RMSF/DIC) requiring immediate blood cultures, IV antibiotics, and shock resuscitation [Ref 14, 32].

quiz.text: Which triad constitutes the bedside qSOFA screening score for high-risk sepsis mortality?
quiz.stem: Which triad constitutes the bedside qSOFA screening score for high-risk sepsis mortality?
options: Fever >38°C, WBC >12,000, HR >90
Respiratory rate >=22/min, Altered mentation (GCS <15), Systolic BP <=100 mmHg
Hemoglobin <10, Platelets <100k, Bilirubin >2
Cough, sputum, and chest crackles
hints: qSOFA requires zero laboratory tests — only 3 bedside clinical signs.
Remember: Breathing fast, Brain confused, BP low.
RR >=22, GCS <15, SBP <=100 mmHg [Ref 32].
quiz.rationale: qSOFA uses three rapid bedside variables (RR >=22/min, altered mentation, SBP <=100 mmHg); a score >=2 flags patients with suspected infection at high risk of ICU admission or death [Ref 32].

quiz.text: Which central hypothalamic mediator is synthesized in response to pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) to raise the body's thermoregulatory set-point?
quiz.stem: Which central hypothalamic mediator is synthesized in response to pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) to raise the body's thermoregulatory set-point?
options: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT)
Histamine H1 in the medulla
Dopamine in the substantia nigra
Aldosterone in the adrenal cortex
hints: Why do aspirin and NSAIDs reduce fever?
They inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX), blocking synthesis of a specific prostaglandin.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 20 identifies PGE2 acting on preoptic hypothalamic neurons as the final fever mediator.
quiz.rationale: Exogenous pyrogens stimulate host cells to release pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, IFN), triggering endothelial COX-2 production of PGE2 near the preoptic hypothalamus to elevate the thermal set-point [Ref 13].

quiz.text: A patient presents with fever, headache, and a maculopapular rash that began on the WRISTS AND ANKLES and spread centripetally to the palms, soles, and trunk, becoming petechial. Which empiric therapy must be started immediately?
quiz.stem: A patient presents with fever, headache, and a maculopapular rash that began on the WRISTS AND ANKLES and spread centripetally to the palms, soles, and trunk, becoming petechial. Which empiric therapy must be started immediately?
options: Oral cephalexin
Doxycycline (for suspected Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever / rickettsiosis)
Topical hydrocortisone cream
Oral fluconazole
hints: Centripetal rash starting on wrists/ankles involving palms & soles + fever -> think tick-borne rickettsia!
Rickettsia rickettsii (RMSF) is fatal if doxycycline is delayed past day 5.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 21 highlights doxycycline as the treatment of choice across all ages.
quiz.rationale: A centripetal rash starting on wrists/ankles and involving palms/soles with fever and headache is classic for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (Rickettsia rickettsii); immediate doxycycline is life-saving [Ref 14].

quiz.text: Under classic criteria in Harrison's 22e Ch. 22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), what defines Classic Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO)?
quiz.stem: Under classic criteria in Harrison's 22e Ch. 22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), what defines Classic Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO)?
options: Any fever >38.0°C lasting 48 hours
Fever >=38.3°C (>=101°F) on multiple occasions for >=3 weeks without diagnosis despite structured minimal diagnostic workup
Fever in a patient who just returned from a 2-day flight
Fever resolving with acetaminophen
hints: Recall Petersdorf & Beeson's core temperature and duration thresholds updated in 22e.
Temperature >=38.3°C lasting at least 3 weeks.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 22 replaces '1 week inpatient stay' with a standardized minimal diagnostic checklist.
quiz.rationale: Classic FUO requires fever >=38.3°C (101°F) for >=3 weeks with no diagnosis despite an obligatory structured baseline evaluation (history, exam, labs, blood cultures, CXR/abdominal imaging) [Ref 15].

quiz.text: A patient with Classic FUO has undergone negative baseline labs, blood cultures, CT chest/abdomen, and autoimmune serologies without any Potentially Diagnostic Clues (PDCs). Which imaging modality has the highest diagnostic yield in modern FUO protocols (Ch. 22)?
quiz.stem: A patient with Classic FUO has undergone negative baseline labs, blood cultures, CT chest/abdomen, and autoimmune serologies without any Potentially Diagnostic Clues (PDCs). Which imaging modality has the highest diagnostic yield in modern FUO protocols (Ch. 22)?
options: Repeat plain chest radiograph
18F-FDG-PET/CT to localize occult large-vessel vasculitis, deep abscesses, or lymphoma
Routine bone marrow biopsy in all asymptomatic patients before imaging
Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics before localization
hints: Think about functional molecular imaging that highlights both occult inflammation (giant cell arteritis/Takayasu) and malignancy.
FDG-PET/CT detects metabolically active foci across the whole body.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 22 recommends FDG-PET/CT early when baseline workup lacks localizing clues.
quiz.rationale: 18F-FDG-PET/CT has a ~50–60% helpful diagnostic yield in FUO by localizing large-vessel vasculitis, hidden deep infections, and occult lymphomas for targeted biopsy [Ref 15].

quiz.text: In a patient with cirrhosis who ate raw oysters 24 hours ago and now presents with fever, septic shock, and hemorrhagic bullae on the legs, which pathogen and therapy must be targeted immediately?
quiz.stem: In a patient with cirrhosis who ate raw oysters 24 hours ago and now presents with fever, septic shock, and hemorrhagic bullae on the legs, which pathogen and therapy must be targeted immediately?
options: Vibrio vulnificus — immediate IV Doxycycline + 3rd-generation cephalosporin (e.g., Ceftriaxone/Cefotaxime) + surgical evaluation
Staphylococcus epidermidis — oral dicloxacillin
Parvovirus B19 — supportive fluids only
Borrelia burgdorferi — oral amoxicillin
hints: Cirrhosis/iron overload + seawater or raw oysters + fulminant hemorrhagic bullae!
Think of a halophilic Gram-negative marine bacillus.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 21 highlights Vibrio vulnificus septicemia with hemorrhagic bullae.
quiz.rationale: Vibrio vulnificus causes rapidly lethal septicemia with hemorrhagic bullae in patients with cirrhosis or hemochromatosis after raw shellfish ingestion or seawater exposure; immediate IV doxycycline + ceftriaxone is required [Ref 14].

quiz.text: Why is empiric 'therapeutic trial' of glucocorticoids or broad-spectrum antibiotics generally DISCOURAGED in stable patients with Classic FUO (Ch. 22)?
quiz.stem: Why is empiric 'therapeutic trial' of glucocorticoids or broad-spectrum antibiotics generally DISCOURAGED in stable patients with Classic FUO (Ch. 22)?
options: Because empiric steroids/antibiotics obscure tissue histology (e.g., lymphoma), sterilize cultures (e.g., endocarditis/TB), and can worsen occult disseminated infections
Because steroids never lower fever
Because FUO resolves spontaneously within 24 hours
Because antibiotics are ineffective in bacterial infections
hints: Think about what happens to a lymph node biopsy or disseminated tuberculosis if you give prednisone blindly.
Masking the fever does not cure the underlying pathology and delays definitive diagnosis.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 22 restricts empiric therapy in FUO to unstable/neutropenic patients or suspected temporal arteritis with vision threat.
quiz.rationale: In clinically stable FUO patients, empiric antimicrobials or glucocorticoids frequently mask diagnostic clues (e.g., delaying TB, endocarditis, or lymphoma diagnosis) and worsen outcomes [Ref 15].

points.title: Four Major Diagnostic Categories of Classic FUO (Ch. 22) [Ref 15]
rows: Extrapulmonary TB, Culture-negative Endocarditis, Occult Abscesses, Enteric Fever, Brucellosis
Travel/animal exposures, cardiac murmurs, night sweats, immunocompromised state
Giant Cell Arteritis (elderly), Adult-Onset Still's Disease, SLE, Polyarteritis Nodosa
Jaw claudication, salmon-pink evanescent rash, markedly elevated ferritin/ESR
Lymphoma (Hodgkin/NHL), Renal Cell Carcinoma, Leukemia, Hepatic/Atrial Myxoma
B-symptoms, lymphadenopathy, elevated LDH, microscopic hematuria
Drug fever (beta-lactams, anticonvulsants, sulfonamides), PE, Factitious fever
Relative bradycardia (pulse-temp dissociation), eosinophilia, resolution on drug withdrawal

points.title: Faget's Sign, Relative Bradycardia & Hyperthermia Syndromes [Ref 13, 14]
points.body: Normally heart rate rises ~10–15 bpm per 1°C rise in temperature. **Relative bradycardia (temperature-pulse dissociation)** points toward **enteric fever (typhoid), Legionella, brucellosis, drug fever, or CNS lesions**. Always separate **malignant hyperthermia** (anesthetics -> IV **dantrolene**), **NMS** (antipsychotics, lead-pipe rigidity -> dantrolene/bromocriptine), and **serotonin syndrome** (SSRIs/linezolid, hyperreflexia & clonus -> benzodiazepines/cyproheptadine).

units.title: Approach to Pain, Acute Chest Discomfort & Abdominal Pain
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 14, 15 & 16 — 6 Lethal Chest Causes, Acute Abdomen & Multimodal Analgesia

points.title: The 6 Immediately Life-Threatening Causes of Acute Chest Discomfort [Ref 11, 31]
rows: Retrosternal pressure/heaviness radiating to jaw/left arm + diaphoresis
12-lead ECG <=10 min, Aspirin, serial hs-cTn, PCI <90 min for STEMI
Abrupt maximal 'tearing/ripping' pain to interscapular back; >20 mmHg arm BP diff; AR murmur
STOP anticoagulants! IV Beta-blocker FIRST (HR <60, SBP 100-120) + stat CTA
Sudden pleuritic pain + dyspnea + tachycardia/hypoxemia; unilateral leg swelling
Sudden pleuritic pain + severe dyspnea + hypotension + unilateral absent breath sounds
Immediate needle decompression (do NOT await CXR!) -> chest tube
Chest discomfort + Beck's triad (hypotension, high JVP, muffled sounds) + pulsus paradoxus
Sudden severe chest/epigastric pain after forceful vomiting; subcutaneous emphysema
NPO, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, water-soluble contrast esophagram/CT, surgical consult

points.title: Visceral vs Parietal vs Referred Abdominal Pain [Ref 12]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 16 (Jacobs) [Ref 12]:** **Visceral pain** (hollow organ stretch/ischemia) is dull, poorly localized, and **midline** (foregut = epigastric, midgut = periumbilical, hindgut = suprapubic). Once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, **somatic/parietal pain** becomes sharp, sharply localized (e.g., McBurney's point in appendicitis), and worsens with coughing or movement (guarding/rebound). **Crucial Rule:** Judicious IV opioid analgesia **DOES NOT** mask peritoneal signs or impair diagnostic accuracy!

quiz.text: Within what maximum time window from arrival must a 12-lead ECG be acquired and interpreted in any adult presenting with acute nontraumatic chest discomfort?
quiz.stem: Within what maximum time window from arrival must a 12-lead ECG be acquired and interpreted in any adult presenting with acute nontraumatic chest discomfort?
options: Within 10 minutes
Within 60 minutes
Within 4 hours after troponin returns
Only if pain lasts >24 hours
hints: Time is myocardium in STEMI!
AHA/ACC 2021 & Harrison's 22e Ch. 15 establish a strict door-to-ECG benchmark.
10 minutes is the universal emergency quality metric.
quiz.rationale: Both Harrison's 22e Ch. 15 [Ref 11] and the 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline [Ref 31] mandate acquiring and interpreting a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of patient arrival.

quiz.text: A 65-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden, maximal 'ripping' substernal pain radiating straight between his shoulder blades. Right arm BP is 190/104 mmHg; left arm BP is 148/82 mmHg. What is the mandatory FIRST class of IV medication?
quiz.stem: A 65-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden, maximal 'ripping' substernal pain radiating straight between his shoulder blades. Right arm BP is 190/104 mmHg; left arm BP is 148/82 mmHg. What is the mandatory FIRST class of IV medication?
options: IV Heparin + Fibrinolytic therapy
IV Beta-blocker (Esmolol or Labetalol) to reduce heart rate (<60 bpm) and shear stress (dP/dt)
IV Nitroprusside alone without beta-blockade
High-dose oral NSAIDs
hints: This is classic Acute Aortic Dissection!
Never give anticoagulants or unopposed vasodilators first.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 15 requires IV beta-blockade FIRST (HR <60, SBP 100–120 mmHg) to lower wall shear stress.
quiz.rationale: In suspected acute aortic dissection, IV beta-blockers (esmolol/labetalol) MUST be given BEFORE vasodilators to prevent reflex tachycardia and lower aortic wall dP/dt shear stress [Ref 11].

quiz.text: Why does acute appendicitis classically begin as dull periumbilical pain and migrate several hours later to sharp right lower quadrant (McBurney's point) pain?
quiz.stem: Why does acute appendicitis classically begin as dull periumbilical pain and migrate several hours later to sharp right lower quadrant (McBurney's point) pain?
options: Because the appendix physically moves across the abdomen
Early luminal distension triggers midline midgut visceral pain; transmural inflammation later irritates localized somatic parietal peritoneum
Because oral painkillers shift the pain location
Because appendicitis is always a referred pain from the diaphragm
hints: Distinguish visceral afferent fibers (midgut = periumbilical) from somatic parietal peritoneal nerves.
Midgut embryologic structures refer visceral pain to the umbilicus.
Parietal peritoneal irritation produces sharp, precisely localized pain with guarding [Ch. 16].
quiz.rationale: Early appendiceal distension produces vague midline midgut visceral pain (periumbilical); once inflammation contacts the adjacent parietal peritoneum, somatic afferents produce sharp RLQ pain [Ref 12].

quiz.text: A patient presents with severe acute abdominal pain and suspected appendicitis while awaiting surgical evaluation. Should cautious titrated IV opioid analgesia be withheld until the surgeon examines the patient?
quiz.stem: A patient presents with severe acute abdominal pain and suspected appendicitis while awaiting surgical evaluation. Should cautious titrated IV opioid analgesia be withheld until the surgeon examines the patient?
options: Yes — opioids always hide peritonitis and cause missed surgeries
No — Harrison's 22e Ch. 16 confirms that judicious opioid analgesia relieves suffering WITHOUT masking peritoneal signs or increasing diagnostic errors
Yes — only give oral antacids until CT is read
No — give high-dose oral NSAIDs instead of IV analgesia
hints: This is a famous historical surgical myth overturned by RCTs!
Gentle pain relief often makes the abdominal exam MORE reliable by reducing voluntary guarding.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 16 explicitly recommends humane, judicious analgesia during evaluation.
quiz.rationale: Randomized trials summarized in Harrison's 22e Ch. 16 [Ref 12] prove that judicious IV opioid analgesia relieves acute pain without obscuring peritoneal signs or impairing surgical decision-making.

quiz.text: A 68-year-old smoker with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, agonizing generalized abdominal pain ('pain out of proportion to physical exam') with a soft, non-tender abdomen and lactate 4.8 mmol/L. What is the leading diagnosis?
quiz.stem: A 68-year-old smoker with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, agonizing generalized abdominal pain ('pain out of proportion to physical exam') with a soft, non-tender abdomen and lactate 4.8 mmol/L. What is the leading diagnosis?
options: Irritable bowel syndrome
Acute Mesenteric Ischemia
Uncomplicated peptic ulcer disease
Chronic constipation
hints: Atrial fibrillation = embolic source; 'pain out of proportion to exam' + elevated lactate!
Before bowel infarction causes peritonitis, the abdomen remains paradoxically soft.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 16 highlights acute mesenteric ischemia as a high-mortality vascular emergency.
quiz.rationale: 'Pain out of proportion to physical examination' in a patient with atrial fibrillation/atherosclerosis and lactic acidosis is the classic presentation of Acute Mesenteric Ischemia requiring emergent CTA [Ref 12].

quiz.text: Which ECG and physical exam pattern strongly favors Acute Pericarditis over acute STEMI?
quiz.stem: Which ECG and physical exam pattern strongly favors Acute Pericarditis over acute STEMI?
options: Localized ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL
Pleuritic chest pain improved by leaning forward, pericardial friction rub, and DIFFUSE concave ST elevation with PR-segment depression (PR elevation in aVR)
New right bundle branch block with hypotension
Deep Q waves in V1–V4
hints: Think about positional relief and diffuse non-territorial ECG changes.
Leaning forward relieves pericardial friction against the pleura/diaphragm.
Diffuse ST elevation + PR depression without reciprocal territorial depressions points to pericarditis [Ch. 15].
quiz.rationale: Acute pericarditis classically causes sharp pleuritic pain relieved by sitting up/leaning forward, a scratchy friction rub, and diffuse concave-up ST elevations with PR depression [Ref 11].

quiz.text: Which extra-abdominal medical emergencies MUST always be considered in a patient presenting with acute epigastric or diffuse abdominal pain (Ch. 16)?
quiz.stem: Which extra-abdominal medical emergencies MUST always be considered in a patient presenting with acute epigastric or diffuse abdominal pain (Ch. 16)?
options: Inferior myocardial infarction, Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), lower-lobe pneumonia, and ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)
Migraine headache and cataracts
Carpal tunnel syndrome and plantar fasciitis
Essential tremor and gout of the great toe
hints: Never forget cardiac, metabolic, pulmonary, and retroperitoneal vascular mimics of an 'acute abdomen'!
Inferior wall MI frequently presents with isolated epigastric pain and nausea in diabetics and older adults.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 16 mandates ECG, glucose/ketones, and AAA evaluation when indicated.
quiz.rationale: Inferior MI, DKA, lower-lobe pneumonia, and leaking/ruptured AAA frequently masquerade as primary intra-abdominal pain and must never be overlooked [Ref 12].

quiz.text: In neuropathic pain (e.g., painful diabetic neuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia), which drug classes are recommended as FIRST-LINE therapy in Harrison's 22e Ch. 14 (Rathmell & Fields)?
quiz.stem: In neuropathic pain (e.g., painful diabetic neuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia), which drug classes are recommended as FIRST-LINE therapy in Harrison's 22e Ch. 14 (Rathmell & Fields)?
options: High-dose immediate-release oxycodone monotherapy
Gabapentinoids (gabapentin/pregabalin), SNRIs (duloxetine/venlafaxine), TCAs (nortriptyline/amitriptyline), or topical lidocaine
Oral acetaminophen 4 g/day alone
Oral corticosteroids
hints: Neuropathic pain responds poorly to NSAIDs and requires modulation of central/peripheral neural excitability.
Recall the non-opioid first-line pharmacologic pillars in Ch. 14.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 14 designates gabapentinoids, SNRIs, and TCAs as first-line over opioids.
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 14 [Ref 10] specifies gabapentinoids, SNRIs (duloxetine), tricyclic antidepressants, and topical lidocaine as first-line agents for neuropathic pain, reserving opioids as second/third-line due to tolerance and overdose risk.

quiz.text: Which primary afferent nerve fibers mediate rapid, sharp, well-localized 'first pain' vs slow, dull, burning 'second pain'?
quiz.stem: Which primary afferent nerve fibers mediate rapid, sharp, well-localized 'first pain' vs slow, dull, burning 'second pain'?
options: Myelinated A-delta fibers mediate sharp fast pain; unmyelinated C fibers mediate slow dull/burning pain
A-beta fibers mediate all visceral pain; C fibers mediate vibration
Unmyelinated C fibers conduct faster than A-delta fibers
Motor alpha neurons transmit nociception
hints: Myelination increases conduction velocity.
A-delta (thinly myelinated) = fast sharp localization; C fibers (unmyelinated) = slow aching/burning.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 14 details peripheral nociceptor physiology in Section 1.
quiz.rationale: Thinly myelinated A-delta nociceptors conduct fast, sharp, well-localized pain, while unmyelinated polymodal C fibers transmit slower, poorly localized aching or burning pain [Ref 10].

quiz.text: A 55-year-old man develops sudden excruciating retrosternal chest pain and subcutaneous crepitus in the neck immediately after violent retching following alcohol intake. Chest X-ray shows left pleural effusion and pneumomediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.stem: A 55-year-old man develops sudden excruciating retrosternal chest pain and subcutaneous crepitus in the neck immediately after violent retching following alcohol intake. Chest X-ray shows left pleural effusion and pneumomediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
options: Boerhaave syndrome (transmural esophageal rupture)
Mallory-Weiss mucosal tear
Unstable angina
Costochondritis
hints: Forceful emesis + pneumomediastinum + subcutaneous emphysema + left pleural effusion (Mackler triad)!
Unlike Mallory-Weiss (mucosal bleed), this is a full-thickness perforation spilling gastric contents into the mediastinum.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 15 lists esophageal rupture among the 6 lethal causes of chest discomfort.
quiz.rationale: Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous transmural esophageal perforation after forceful vomiting) causes mediastinitis, subcutaneous emphysema, and left pleural effusion, requiring emergent NPO, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and surgical repair [Ref 11].

quiz.text: Which adverse effect of scheduled opioid analgesics NEVER develops tolerance and requires proactive prophylactic prescribing from Day 1 (Ch. 14)?
quiz.stem: Which adverse effect of scheduled opioid analgesics NEVER develops tolerance and requires proactive prophylactic prescribing from Day 1 (Ch. 14)?
options: Sedation
Nausea
Opioid-induced constipation
Mild pruritus
hints: Patients adapt to mild drowsiness and nausea within days, but gut mu-receptors NEVER adapt!
Always co-prescribe a stimulant laxative (e.g., senna/PEG) when starting scheduled opioids.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 14 highlights prophylactic bowel regimens as mandatory opioid stewardship [Ref 10].
quiz.rationale: Unlike sedation and nausea, tolerance virtually never develops to opioid-induced constipation; prophylactic laxative therapy must accompany every scheduled opioid regimen [Ref 10].

points.title: High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin (hs-cTn) Serial Kinetics [Ref 11, 31]
points.body: Modern **0/1-hour** and **0/2-hour hs-cTn algorithms** distinguish **acute myocardial injury** (dynamic rise/fall >20%) from **chronic myocardial injury** (stable elevation in CKD, CHF, LVH). Remember: troponin indicates myocyte injury, NOT solely plaque rupture — distinguish **Type 1 MI** (thrombotic ACS) from **Type 2 MI** (supply-demand mismatch in sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, or severe anemia).

points.title: Acute Abdomen Red Flags Requiring Urgent Surgical Evaluation [Ref 12]
points.body: Board-like rigidity, involuntary guarding, hemodynamic instability, free subdiaphragmatic air on upright CXR/CT, pulsatile tender abdominal mass (ruptured AAA), positive urine hCG with pelvic pain/hypotension (ruptured ectopic pregnancy), and pain out of proportion to exam (mesenteric ischemia).

points.title: Multimodal Analgesia & Descending Pain Modulation [Ref 10]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 14**, pain signals ascend via the **spinothalamic tract** and are modulated by descending serotonergic/noradrenergic pathways from the **periaqueductal gray (PAG)** and **rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM)** — explaining why SNRIs and TCAs reduce chronic pain independent of mood effects.

units.title: Approach to Dyspnea, Hypoxia, Cyanosis & Edema
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 39, 42 & 43 — 5 Mechanisms of Hypoxemia, A–a Gradient, Cyanosis & Starling Forces

points.title: The 5 Mechanisms of Hypoxemia Differentiated by A–a Gradient [Ref 20]
rows: Opioid overdose, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barré, obesity hypoventilation
COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, interstitial disease
ARDS, dense lobar pneumonia/atelectasis, pulmonary AVM, intracardiac R->L shunt

points.title: Cyanosis Cutoff (Harrison's 22e Ch. 42) & The Severe Anemia Trap [Ref 20]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 42 (Loscalzo) [Ref 20]:** Visible cyanosis appears when capillary **reduced (deoxygenated) hemoglobin exceeds 40 g/L (4 g/dL)**. Because cyanosis depends on the **ABSOLUTE** amount of deoxyhemoglobin, a severely anemic patient (e.g., Hb 5 g/dL) may suffer fatal tissue hypoxia **WITHOUT ever turning cyanotic**! Conversely, **polycythemia** causes cyanosis at mild desaturation. **Central cyanosis** involves warm tongue/oral mucosa (cardiopulmonary/shunt/metHb); **peripheral cyanosis** spares the tongue (vasoconstriction/cold/low CO).

points.title: Clinical Localization of Generalized Edema via JVP & Starling Forces [Ref 21]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 43 (Loscalzo) [Ref 21]**, edema reflects imbalance in **Starling forces** (capillary hydrostatic vs plasma oncotic pressure + permeability + lymphatic drainage) amplified by renal Na⁺/water retention via **RAAS** when effective arterial blood volume (EABV) falls. **Check the JVP first:** Elevated JVP -> **Heart Failure** or **Renal overload**; Normal/Low JVP -> **Cirrhosis** (ascites > leg edema) or **Nephrotic Syndrome** (periorbital edema + heavy proteinuria).

quiz.text: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 42 (Loscalzo), why can a patient with severe anemia (Hb 4.5 g/dL) be profoundly hypoxic yet show NO visible cyanosis?
quiz.stem: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 42 (Loscalzo), why can a patient with severe anemia (Hb 4.5 g/dL) be profoundly hypoxic yet show NO visible cyanosis?
options: Anemic blood carries extra dissolved oxygen
Cyanosis requires >4 g/dL (40 g/L) of ABSOLUTE deoxygenated hemoglobin in capillaries, which is nearly impossible to reach when total Hb is 4.5 g/dL
Pulse oximetry turns blue skin pink
Cyanosis only occurs in carbon monoxide poisoning
hints: Does cyanosis depend on oxygen saturation percentage OR absolute grams/dL of deoxyhemoglobin?
At total Hb 4.5 g/dL, reaching >4 g/dL deoxyhemoglobin would mean <11% SpO2 (incompatible with life).
Harrison's 22e Ch. 42 explicitly states >40 g/L (4 g/dL) reduced hemoglobin is needed.
quiz.rationale: Visible cyanosis requires >4 g/dL (40 g/L) of absolute capillary deoxyhemoglobin; severely anemic patients lack sufficient total hemoglobin to appear cyanotic even during critical hypoxia [Ref 20].

quiz.text: How do you rapidly distinguish CENTRAL cyanosis from PERIPHERAL cyanosis at the bedside?
quiz.stem: How do you rapidly distinguish CENTRAL cyanosis from PERIPHERAL cyanosis at the bedside?
options: Inspect the tongue and oral mucous membranes: central cyanosis turns the warm tongue/mucosa blue, whereas peripheral cyanosis spares the tongue and affects cool digits/nail beds
Check finger temperature only
Peripheral cyanosis always lowers PaO2 below 40 mmHg
Central cyanosis only affects the toes
hints: Where is blood flow warm and unaffected by cold-induced vasoconstriction?
The tongue and sublingual mucosa!
Central = arterial desaturation (tongue + extremities); Peripheral = sluggish capillary extraction (cool extremities, pink tongue) [Ch. 42].
quiz.rationale: Central cyanosis involves both warm mucous membranes (tongue/lips) and extremities due to arterial desaturation or abnormal hemoglobin; peripheral cyanosis spares the tongue and reflects low cardiac output or vasoconstriction [Ref 20].

quiz.text: A patient presents with acute progressive dyspnea, orthopnea (sleeping on 3 pillows), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), bilateral basal crackles, and elevated JVP. Which primary system is driving the dyspnea?
quiz.stem: A patient presents with acute progressive dyspnea, orthopnea (sleeping on 3 pillows), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), bilateral basal crackles, and elevated JVP. Which primary system is driving the dyspnea?
options: Cardiovascular — acute decompensated left heart failure / pulmonary venous congestion
Isolated iron-deficiency anemia
Psychogenic hyperventilation
Primary nephrotic syndrome without volume overload
hints: Orthopnea + PND + elevated JVP + basal crackles!
Lying flat redistributes ~500 mL of fluid into the central pulmonary circulation.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 39 & 43 link orthopnea/PND + elevated JVP to left ventricular congestion.
quiz.rationale: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea with elevated JVP and basal crackles are hallmark signs of left-sided heart failure causing interstitial pulmonary edema [Ref 19, 21].

quiz.text: A patient taking amlodipine (dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) develops bilateral pitting ankle edema with normal JVP, clear lungs, normal BNP, normal serum albumin, and no proteinuria. What is the mechanism?
quiz.stem: A patient taking amlodipine (dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) develops bilateral pitting ankle edema with normal JVP, clear lungs, normal BNP, normal serum albumin, and no proteinuria. What is the mechanism?
options: Preferential precapillary arteriolar vasodilation increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure
Severe hypoalbuminemia from liver failure
Right ventricular infarction
Lymphatic obstruction from filariasis
hints: Think about Starling forces when arterioles dilate more than venules.
Higher pressure transmits into the capillary bed, pushing fluid into the interstitium without total body sodium overload.
Loop diuretics work poorly here — switching/adding an ACEi/ARB (which dilates postcapillary venules) resolves it [Ch. 43].
quiz.rationale: Dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine/nifedipine) selectively dilate precapillary arterioles, elevating capillary hydrostatic pressure and causing benign peripheral edema without elevated JVP [Ref 21].

quiz.text: Which mechanism of hypoxemia is characterized by an ELEVATED A–a O2 gradient that FAILS to correct even with 100% inspired oxygen (FiO2 1.0)?
quiz.stem: Which mechanism of hypoxemia is characterized by an ELEVATED A–a O2 gradient that FAILS to correct even with 100% inspired oxygen (FiO2 1.0)?
options: Alveolar hypoventilation
Right-to-Left Shunt (e.g., ARDS, dense lobar consolidation, or intracardiac shunt)
High altitude exposure
Mild V/Q mismatch in asthma
hints: Think: if blood bypasses ventilated alveoli completely, does adding more oxygen to the alveoli reach that shunted blood?
No! Shunted venous blood never sees the 100% oxygen.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 42 defines refractoriness to 100% O2 as the hallmark of right-to-left shunt.
quiz.rationale: In a right-to-left shunt, deoxygenated blood bypasses gas-exchanging alveoli completely, so raising FiO2 to 100% cannot oxygenate the shunted fraction [Ref 20].

quiz.text: A 48-year-old man found somnolent after an opioid overdose has room-air ABG: pH 7.22, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 52 mmHg (PAO2 ≈ 65 mmHg; expected normal A–a gradient <=16 mmHg). What is the A–a gradient and mechanism?
quiz.stem: A 48-year-old man found somnolent after an opioid overdose has room-air ABG: pH 7.22, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 52 mmHg (PAO2 ≈ 65 mmHg; expected normal A–a gradient <=16 mmHg). What is the A–a gradient and mechanism?
options: A–a gradient = 13 mmHg (Normal) -> Pure Alveolar Hypoventilation
A–a gradient = 45 mmHg (Elevated) -> Pulmonary Embolism
A–a gradient = 13 mmHg -> Right-to-left shunt
A–a gradient = 0 mmHg -> Carbon monoxide toxicity
hints: Subtract PaO2 from PAO2: 65 − 52 = 13 mmHg.
Compare 13 mmHg to age-expected normal (48/4 + 4 = 16 mmHg).
Normal A–a gradient + elevated PaCO2 = pure alveolar hypoventilation [Ch. 42].
quiz.rationale: The A–a gradient is 65 − 52 = 13 mmHg (normal <=16 mmHg for age 48). Combined with PaCO2 68 mmHg, this confirms pure alveolar hypoventilation from opioid CNS depression [Ref 20].

quiz.text: In a patient with generalized edema, which bedside/laboratory constellation distinguishes Nephrotic Syndrome from Cirrhosis?
quiz.stem: In a patient with generalized edema, which bedside/laboratory constellation distinguishes Nephrotic Syndrome from Cirrhosis?
options: Prominent periorbital edema, frothy urine (>3.5 g/day proteinuria), hyperlipidemia, and normal JVP -> Nephrotic Syndrome
Marked ascites preceding ankle edema, spider angiomata, and splenomegaly -> Nephrotic Syndrome
Elevated JVP with S3 gallop -> Nephrotic Syndrome
Unilateral warm swollen calf -> Nephrotic Syndrome
hints: Where does low-oncotic edema accumulate first due to low tissue tension?
Periorbital soft tissues (especially on waking) + heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/d) + hyperlipidemia.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 43 contrasts nephrotic, cirrhotic, and cardiac edema patterns.
quiz.rationale: Nephrotic syndrome causes marked hypoalbuminemia with periorbital and dependent pitting edema, heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/24h), and hyperlipidemia without elevated JVP [Ref 21].

quiz.text: A patient develops chocolate-brown arterial blood and central cyanosis unresponsive to 100% O2 after topical benzocaine spray for TEE. Pulse oximetry stubbornly reads 85% despite arterial PaO2 of 240 mmHg! What is the diagnosis and antidote?
quiz.stem: A patient develops chocolate-brown arterial blood and central cyanosis unresponsive to 100% O2 after topical benzocaine spray for TEE. Pulse oximetry stubbornly reads 85% despite arterial PaO2 of 240 mmHg! What is the diagnosis and antidote?
options: Methemoglobinemia (Hb Fe3+) — administer IV Methylene Blue
Carbon monoxide poisoning — administer hyperbaric oxygen
Massive pulmonary embolism — administer alteplase
Cyanide toxicity — administer hydroxocobalamin
hints: Normal/high PaO2 + SpO2 stuck around ~85% ('saturation gap') + chocolate-brown blood after benzocaine/dapsone!
Oxidized ferric iron (Fe3+) cannot bind O2 and shifts the O2-Hb curve left.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 42 identifies methemoglobinemia treated with IV methylene blue.
quiz.rationale: Benzocaine oxidizes heme iron from Fe2+ to Fe3+ (methemoglobin), causing central cyanosis refractory to O2, SpO2 fixed near 85% with high PaO2, chocolate blood, and rapid reversal with IV methylene blue [Ref 20].

quiz.text: What is 'platypnea–orthodeoxia' and what classic vascular abnormality does it signify (Harrison's 22e Ch. 39 & 42)?
quiz.stem: What is 'platypnea–orthodeoxia' and what classic vascular abnormality does it signify (Harrison's 22e Ch. 39 & 42)?
options: Dyspnea and arterial desaturation that WORSEN when upright and IMPROVE when lying flat — classic for Hepatopulmonary Syndrome (intrapulmonary shunts) or PFO
Dyspnea occurring only when lying flat — classic for left heart failure
Dyspnea exclusively during REM sleep
Wheezing triggered by cold air
hints: Notice the opposite of orthopnea!
Gravity increases blood flow through dilated basilar pulmonary capillaries (shunt) when standing upright.
Classic for Hepatopulmonary Syndrome in cirrhosis or patent foramen ovale [Ch. 39, 42].
quiz.rationale: Platypnea (dyspnea when upright) with orthodeoxia (drop in PaO2/SpO2 when upright) occurs when gravity increases right-to-left shunting through basilar intrapulmonary vasodilations in hepatopulmonary syndrome or atrial septal defects [Ref 19, 20].

quiz.text: Why do patients with Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning typically have a NORMAL arterial PaO2 AND a falsely normal standard pulse oximetry (SpO2) reading despite lethal cellular hypoxia?
quiz.stem: Why do patients with Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning typically have a NORMAL arterial PaO2 AND a falsely normal standard pulse oximetry (SpO2) reading despite lethal cellular hypoxia?
options: CO binds hemoglobin with >200× affinity of O2 without lowering dissolved PaO2, and standard 2-wavelength pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin
CO directly stimulates alveolar hyperventilation raising PaO2 to 400 mmHg
CO destroys pulmonary capillaries
Pulse oximeters only fail in hypothermia
hints: Distinguish dissolved oxygen (PaO2) from total arterial O2 content (bound to Hb).
Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs red light similarly to oxyhemoglobin on standard 2-wavelength SpO2 probes.
Always order CO-oximetry when CO poisoning is suspected [Ch. 42].
quiz.rationale: CO forms carboxyhemoglobin (reducing O2 carrying capacity and shifting the dissociation curve left) while leaving dissolved PaO2 and standard 2-wavelength SpO2 falsely normal; diagnosis requires arterial CO-oximetry [Ref 20].

quiz.text: Besides decompensated left heart failure, which neuromuscular condition classically produces severe ORTHOPNEA (worsening dyspnea immediately on lying flat)?
quiz.stem: Besides decompensated left heart failure, which neuromuscular condition classically produces severe ORTHOPNEA (worsening dyspnea immediately on lying flat)?
options: Bilateral diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis
Isolated carpal tunnel syndrome
Peripheral sensory neuropathy of the toes
Mild tension headache
hints: Think about what abdominal organs push against when you lie flat without diaphragmatic tone!
Abdominal contents displace the paralyzed diaphragm upward into the thorax, slashing vital capacity.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 39 notes bilateral diaphragm paralysis as a classic non-cardiac cause of orthopnea [Ref 19].
quiz.rationale: In bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis, lying supine allows abdominal viscera to push the weakened diaphragm cephalad, causing marked orthopnea and paradoxical inward abdominal motion on inspiration [Ref 19].

quiz.text: A 55-year-old presents with acute UNILATERAL warm, tender, pitting right calf swelling (3.5 cm larger than the left) after a 14-hour flight. What is the single most critical first rule from Ch. 43?
quiz.stem: A 55-year-old presents with acute UNILATERAL warm, tender, pitting right calf swelling (3.5 cm larger than the left) after a 14-hour flight. What is the single most critical first rule from Ch. 43?
options: Start oral furosemide for presumed congestive heart failure
NEVER attribute unilateral leg edema to CHF — urgently evaluate for Deep Vein Thrombosis (Wells score + venous compression ultrasound)!
Prescribe compression stockings without imaging
Reassure that it is amlodipine edema
hints: Systemic causes (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic) produce BILATERAL symmetric edema.
Unilateral acute swelling = local venous/lymphatic/inflammatory obstruction (DVT or cellulitis)!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 43 stresses ruling out DVT immediately in unilateral leg edema [Ref 21].
quiz.rationale: Generalized systemic disorders cause bilateral symmetric edema; acute unilateral leg swelling mandates immediate evaluation for Deep Vein Thrombosis (venous duplex ultrasound) or cellulitis [Ref 21].

points.title: Alveolar Gas Equation & Expected Age-Adjusted A–a Gradient [Ref 20]
points.body: At sea level ($P_{atm}=760$, $P_{H2O}=47$, $R=0.8$): **PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (713) − (PaCO₂ / 0.8)**. On room air (FiO₂ 0.21), this simplifies to **PAO₂ ≈ 150 − (1.25 × PaCO₂)**. Normal A–a gradient increases with age: **Normal A–a ≤ (Age / 4) + 4 mmHg**.

points.title: Neurophysiology of Dyspnea: Efferent–Reafferent Mismatch [Ref 19]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 39 (Baron)**, dyspnea arises when central respiratory motor drive (corollary discharge from brainstem) exceeds the expected mechanical feedback from chest wall mechanoreceptors, pulmonary stretch receptors, and arterial chemoreceptors (PaCO₂, pH, PaO₂).

points.title: Differential Diagnosis of Unilateral vs Bilateral Edema & Myxedema [Ref 21]
points.body: **Unilateral acute leg edema** = DVT, cellulitis, or ruptured Baker's cyst (NEVER assume CHF!). **Non-pitting edema** = chronic **lymphedema** (Stemmer sign positive) or **pretibial myxedema** (thyroid disease). In **cirrhosis**, avoid overly aggressive loop diuresis (>0.5 kg/d without peripheral edema) to prevent hepatorenal syndrome.

units.title: Approach to Syncope, Confusion, Delirium & Coma
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 23, 29 & 30 — Cardiac vs Reflex Syncope, CAM Delirium & Coma Brainstem Exam

points.title: Three Core Mechanisms of Syncope (Transient Global Cerebral Hypoperfusion) [Ref 16]
rows: Prolonged standing, pain, fear, micturition; warm diaphoresis & nausea prodrome
Benign prognosis; education, hydration, counter-pressure maneuvers
Standing up -> SBP drop >=20 or DBP drop >=10 mmHg within 3 min (volume depletion, drugs, autonomic failure)
Review antihypertensives/diuretics, hydrate, check hematocrit & autonomic neuropathies
EXERTIONAL syncope, supine syncope, NO prodrome, palpitations, family history of sudden death, abnormal ECG
HIGHEST 1-yr mortality! Admit for telemetry, echocardiogram & electrophysiology!

points.title: Delirium (Acute Fluctuating Attention Disorder) vs Dementia [Ref 17]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 29 (Josephson & Miller) [Ref 17]:** Delirium develops **acutely (hours to days)** with a **fluctuating course** and core **inattention** (Confusion Assessment Method — CAM). **Hypoactive delirium** (quiet, somnolent) is the MOST commonly missed subtype and carries high mortality! Prioritize **non-pharmacologic prevention** (daytime light/wakefulness, eyeglasses/hearing aids, early ambulation, reorientation, discontinuing anticholinergics/benzodiazepines).

points.title: Emergency Coma Stabilization Sequence (First 5 Minutes) [Ref 18]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 30 (Josephson, Ropper & Hauser) [Ref 18]**, coma arises from either **bilateral cerebral hemisphere dysfunction** OR **brainstem ARAS injury**. Immediate order: **(1) ABCs** (intubate if GCS <=8; C-spine if trauma) -> **(2) Stat Glucose + IV Thiamine 100 mg BEFORE/WITH 25g Dextrose** -> **(3) IV Naloxone** if pinpoint pupils/bradypnea -> **(4) Pupils & Brainstem Reflexes** -> **(5) Emergent Head CT**.

quiz.text: Which syncope presentation carries the HIGHEST risk of sudden cardiac death and mandates urgent inpatient telemetry and echocardiography?
