quiz.stem: Which syncope presentation carries the HIGHEST risk of sudden cardiac death and mandates urgent inpatient telemetry and echocardiography?
options: A 22-year-old who feels warm, sweaty, and nauseated after blood draw and faints briefly
A 66-year-old who suddenly collapses WITHOUT prodrome while climbing stairs (exertional syncope) and has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur
A 30-year-old who feels lightheaded after standing quickly from a hot bath
A 19-year-old who faints after prolonged standing in a crowded assembly
hints: Look for red flags: exertion, supine onset, absence of prodrome, structural heart disease!
Harsh systolic murmur + exertional syncope = severe Aortic Stenosis!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 23 identifies cardiac syncope as the highest-mortality category.
quiz.rationale: Exertional syncope without prodrome plus a systolic ejection murmur signifies severe aortic stenosis (or ventricular arrhythmia) — high-risk cardiac syncope requiring immediate inpatient cardiac evaluation [Ref 16].

quiz.text: What blood pressure drop within 3 minutes of standing defines Orthostatic Hypotension in Harrison's 22e Ch. 23?
quiz.stem: What blood pressure drop within 3 minutes of standing defines Orthostatic Hypotension in Harrison's 22e Ch. 23?
options: SBP drop >= 5 mmHg or DBP drop >= 5 mmHg
SBP drop >= 20 mmHg OR DBP drop >= 10 mmHg
SBP drop >= 50 mmHg only
Heart rate increase of 5 bpm without BP change
hints: Recall the standard bedside orthostatic cutoffs.
Systolic >= 20, Diastolic >= 10 within 3 minutes.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 23 uses >=20/10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing.
quiz.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a drop in systolic BP >=20 mmHg or diastolic BP >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing [Ref 16].

quiz.text: What is the single MOST essential feature distinguishing Delirium from Alzheimer's Dementia at the bedside?
quiz.stem: What is the single MOST essential feature distinguishing Delirium from Alzheimer's Dementia at the bedside?
options: Delirium has an ACUTE onset (hours to days) with fluctuating course and impaired attention
Delirium develops slowly over 5 years with normal alertness
Delirium never affects hospitalized older adults
Delirium is permanently irreversible
hints: Compare time course and attention!
Alzheimer's dementia is insidious and progressive over months/years with intact alertness early on.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 29 defines acute onset + fluctuating inattention as the hallmark of delirium.
quiz.rationale: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness developing over hours to days, whereas dementia is chronic and slowly progressive with preserved early attention [Ref 17].

quiz.text: An unresponsive patient (GCS 6) arrives in the ED with unknown history. Bedside glucose is 34 mg/dL. Why should IV Thiamine (100 mg) be given BEFORE or concurrently with 25 g IV Dextrose?
quiz.stem: An unresponsive patient (GCS 6) arrives in the ED with unknown history. Bedside glucose is 34 mg/dL. Why should IV Thiamine (100 mg) be given BEFORE or concurrently with 25 g IV Dextrose?
options: Thiamine increases insulin secretion
In malnourished or alcohol-use patients, a glucose load depletes remaining thiamine stores and can precipitate acute Wernicke encephalopathy
Thiamine lowers blood pressure
Dextrose cannot enter veins without thiamine
hints: Think about pyruvate dehydrogenase cofactor depletion in malnourished patients.
Glucose metabolism consumes thiamine rapidly.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 30 mandates thiamine before/with dextrose (never delaying glucose in proven hypoglycemia).
quiz.rationale: IV thiamine (100 mg) prevents acute precipitation of Wernicke encephalopathy (ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, confusion) when dextrose is infused in thiamine-depleted patients [Ref 18].

quiz.text: Which clinical feature best distinguishes a generalized tonic-clonic SEIZURE from convulsive SYNCOPE?
quiz.stem: Which clinical feature best distinguishes a generalized tonic-clonic SEIZURE from convulsive SYNCOPE?
options: Brief myoclonic jerks lasting <15 seconds
Prolonged postictal confusion (>5–10 minutes), lateral tongue biting, and rhythmic tonic-clonic activity >30–60 seconds
Pale diaphoretic skin before falling
Rapid return to full orientation within 15 seconds of lying flat
hints: Brief myoclonic jerks CAN occur in syncope ('convulsive syncope')!
Look for prolonged postictal confusion and lateral tongue laceration.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 23 contrasts rapid recovery in syncope against prolonged postictal state in seizures.
quiz.rationale: Syncope recovers consciousness rapidly once supine (though brief <15s myoclonus can occur); lateral tongue biting and prolonged postictal confusion strongly favor epileptic seizure [Ref 16].

quiz.text: A comatose patient following head trauma develops a UNILATERAL dilated (7 mm), fixed, unreactive right pupil with contralateral left hemiparesis. What is the anatomic diagnosis and urgent action?
quiz.stem: A comatose patient following head trauma develops a UNILATERAL dilated (7 mm), fixed, unreactive right pupil with contralateral left hemiparesis. What is the anatomic diagnosis and urgent action?
options: Right uncal (transtentorial) herniation compressing CN III and cerebral peduncle — elevate HOB 30°, give IV Mannitol/3% NaCl, emergent Head CT & Neurosurgery STAT
Benign migraine aura — give oral ibuprofen
Opioid overdose — give naloxone only
Hypoglycemia — check glucose tomorrow
hints: Unilateral 'blown' fixed pupil = third cranial nerve (parasympathetic fibers on the outer surface of CN III) compression!
Uncal herniation is an imminent brainstem death emergency.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 30 highlights CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis as classic uncal herniation.
quiz.rationale: A unilateral fixed dilated pupil with coma indicates uncal herniation compressing ipsilateral CN III parasympathetic fibers and the midbrain; immediate ICP-lowering therapy (HOB 30°, hyperosmolar mannitol/3% NaCl) and neurosurgical decompression are mandatory [Ref 18].

quiz.text: Which pupillary finding in a comatose patient strongly points toward a TOXIC-METABOLIC etiology rather than a structural brainstem lesion?
quiz.stem: Which pupillary finding in a comatose patient strongly points toward a TOXIC-METABOLIC etiology rather than a structural brainstem lesion?
options: Bilateral symmetric, briskly reactive pupils despite deep coma
Unilateral 8 mm fixed pupil
Midposition 5 mm fixed unreactive pupils
Skew deviation with absent corneal reflex
hints: Are pupillary light pathways resistant or sensitive to metabolic insults?
Pupillary pathways are remarkably RESISTANT to metabolic/toxic insults!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 30 calls preserved pupillary light reflexes the single most useful bedside sign favoring metabolic coma.
quiz.rationale: Preserved, symmetric pupillary light reflexes in a deeply comatose patient strongly point toward a toxic-metabolic cause (exceptions: anticholinergics/atropine, severe anoxia, or pontine hemorrhage causing pinpoint pupils) [Ref 18].

quiz.text: Which pharmacologic strategy is recommended as FIRST-LINE management for hospital-acquired delirium in Harrison's 22e Ch. 29?
quiz.stem: Which pharmacologic strategy is recommended as FIRST-LINE management for hospital-acquired delirium in Harrison's 22e Ch. 29?
options: Routine scheduled IV lorazepam for all confused elderly patients

Non-pharmacologic multicomponent care (daytime wakefulness, early mobilization, sensory aids, removing offending anticholinergics/sedatives) and treating the underlying trigger; reserve low-dose antipsychotics ONLY for severe dangerous agitation
High-dose diphenhydramine at bedtime to promote sleep
Physical four-point restraints for hypoactive delirium
hints: Remember: benzodiazepines and diphenhydramine (anticholinergic) WORSEN delirium!
Look at the Ch. 29 delirium infographic: shades up, glasses on, walk 3x/day, treat infection/electrolytes.
Antipsychotics are reserved strictly when patients pose an imminent safety threat to themselves or staff [Ch. 29].
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 29 [Ref 17] emphasizes non-pharmacologic reorientation, daytime wakefulness, removing anticholinergics/benzodiazepines, and reversing medical triggers; antipsychotics do not shorten delirium duration and are used only for severe safety-threatening agitation.

quiz.text: A comatose patient presents with PINPOINT (1 mm) pupils that are barely reactive, quadriplegia, absent horizontal oculocephalic (doll's eyes) reflexes, and ocular bobbing. Where is the lesion?
quiz.stem: A comatose patient presents with PINPOINT (1 mm) pupils that are barely reactive, quadriplegia, absent horizontal oculocephalic (doll's eyes) reflexes, and ocular bobbing. Where is the lesion?
options: Acute pontine hemorrhage (or basilar artery pontine infarction)
Left frontal lobe meningioma
Isolated cerebellar vermis lesion
Peripheral diabetic neuropathy
hints: Pinpoint pupils + absent horizontal eye movements (PPRF/CN VI in pons) + ocular bobbing!
Descending sympathetic fibers in the pons are disrupted, leaving unopposed parasympathetic constriction.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 30 localizes pinpoint pupils + absent VOR + ocular bobbing to the pons.
quiz.rationale: Pontine hemorrhage disrupts descending sympathetic tracts (causing pinpoint 1 mm pupils) and horizontal gaze centers/PPRF (abolishing oculocephalic/caloric horizontal reflexes) while producing vertical ocular bobbing [Ref 18].

quiz.text: When performing cold-water oculovestibular (caloric) testing in a comatose patient with an INTACT brainstem, which eye movement response is expected?
quiz.stem: When performing cold-water oculovestibular (caloric) testing in a comatose patient with an INTACT brainstem, which eye movement response is expected?
options: Tonic conjugate deviation of both eyes TOWARD the irrigated cold ear (without fast-phase nystagmus)
Fast-phase nystagmus away from the cold ear (COWS)
No eye movement whatsoever
Vertical upward gaze palsy
hints: Remember COWS: Cold Opposite refers to the FAST corrective phase — which requires an intact cerebral CORTEX!
In coma, the cortex is offline, so only the brainstem-mediated SLOW tonic phase remains.
Intact brainstem in coma = tonic eye deviation TOWARD the cold ear [Ch. 30].
quiz.rationale: In coma (cortical fast phase absent), intact brainstem pathways produce tonic conjugate eye deviation TOWARD the cold-irrigated ear; complete absence of eye movement indicates severe brainstem injury or sedative toxicity [Ref 18].

quiz.text: In which specific delirium scenario ARE benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam/diazepam) the FIRST-LINE pharmacologic therapy rather than contraindicated (Ch. 29)?
quiz.stem: In which specific delirium scenario ARE benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam/diazepam) the FIRST-LINE pharmacologic therapy rather than contraindicated (Ch. 29)?
options: Routine sundowning in Alzheimer's dementia
Alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens) or sedative-hypnotic withdrawal
Hypoactive delirium from urinary tract infection
Post-operative delirium from anticholinergics
hints: Almost all delirium worsens with benzos — except when GABAergic withdrawal IS the cause!
Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal cause lethal excitatory autonomic storm & seizures.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 29 reserves benzodiazepines in delirium specifically for alcohol/sedative withdrawal [Ref 17].
quiz.rationale: While benzodiazepines precipitate or worsen most inpatient delirium, they are life-saving first-line therapy when delirium is driven by alcohol withdrawal (DTs) or benzodiazepine withdrawal [Ref 17].

points.title: High-Risk ECG Red Flags in Syncope (Never Discharge!) [Ref 16]
points.body: Always inspect every syncope ECG for: **Brugada pattern** (coved ST elevation V1–V2), **Long QT** (QTc >480–500 ms), **WPW** (short PR + delta wave), **HOCM** (deep dagger Q waves + LVH), **ARVC** (epsilon wave / TWI V1–V3), and **high-grade AV block / bifascicular block**.

points.title: Coma Brainstem Localization Matrix (Ch. 30) [Ref 18]
rows: Sepsis, uremia, hepatic coma, hyponatremia, hypercapnia
Pontine hemorrhage (absent VOR) vs Opioid (responds to Naloxone)

points.title: Locked-In Syndrome vs Brain Death vs Persistent Vegetative State [Ref 18]
points.body: **Locked-in syndrome** (ventral pontine infarction) preserves consciousness, vertical eye movements, and blinking — ALWAYS ask an apparently comatose patient to look up/down or blink! **Brain death** requires irreversible coma with known cause, exclusion of hypothermia/sedatives/electrolyte mimics, absent brainstem reflexes, and a positive apnea test.

units.title: Approach to GI Bleeding, Jaundice & Ascites
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 51, 52 & 53 — Restrictive Transfusion, Bilirubin Patterns, SAAG & SBP

points.title: Acute Upper GI Bleeding Resuscitation Rules (Ch. 51) [Ref 22, 33]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 51 (Laine) [Ref 22]:** (1) **Early Hemoglobin is FALSELY NORMAL** in acute hemorrhage because plasma and RBCs are lost proportionally—triage by **heart rate, orthostasis, and BP**, NOT initial Hb! (2) **Restrictive PRBC Transfusion at Hb <7 g/dL** reduces rebleeding and mortality compared with liberal transfusion. (3) In suspected **cirrhotic variceal bleeding**, start **IV Octreotide + IV Ceftriaxone** immediately prior to endoscopy (within 12–24h).

points.title: Stepwise Approach to Jaundice (Scleral Icterus >=3.0 mg/dL) [Ref 23]
rows: Overproduction (hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis) or impaired conjugation (Gilbert's)
Reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, peripheral smear (if normal -> Gilbert's syndrome)
Viral hepatitis serologies, acetaminophen/drug levels, ischemic hepatitis ('shock liver'), autoimmune
Immediate RUQ Ultrasound to check bile duct dilation (stones/stricture/pancreatic head mass)

points.title: Diagnostic Paracentesis: SAAG & Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis [Ref 24]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 53 (Friedman) [Ref 24]**, perform diagnostic paracentesis on EVERY patient with new-onset or hospitalized ascites. **SAAG = Serum Albumin − Ascitic Albumin**: **>=1.1 g/dL** = **Portal Hypertension** (cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd-Chiari); **<1.1 g/dL** = **Non-Portal** (peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB peritonitis, pancreatitis, nephrotic). **Ascitic PMN >=250 cells/uL = SBP -> immediate IV Ceftriaxone + IV Albumin!**

quiz.text: A 52-year-old man arrives 20 minutes after vomiting large volumes of bright red blood. His HR is 128 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg, yet his initial Hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL. Why is his hemoglobin NOT low yet?
quiz.stem: A 52-year-old man arrives 20 minutes after vomiting large volumes of bright red blood. His HR is 128 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg, yet his initial Hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL. Why is his hemoglobin NOT low yet?
options: He is not actually bleeding significantly
In acute hemorrhage, whole blood (plasma and RBCs) is lost proportionally; hemoglobin only falls hours later after interstitial fluid shifts or IV crystalloids cause hemodilution
Stomach acid artificially raises hemoglobin measurements
Hemoglobin only drops in lower GI bleeding
hints: Think about concentration (g/dL) when you pour half a cup of coffee out — does the remaining coffee become weaker?
No! Concentration stays identical until water/crystalloid enters the vascular space.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 51 warns clinicians to gauge acute GI bleed severity by hemodynamics (HR/BP), not initial Hb.
quiz.rationale: In acute GI hemorrhage, plasma and red cells are lost in equal proportions, so hemoglobin does not drop immediately until extravascular fluid shifts or IV fluids dilute the remaining RBC mass [Ref 22].

quiz.text: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 51 and ACG 2021 guidelines, what hemoglobin threshold is recommended for packed red blood cell transfusion in most hemodynamically stabilized patients with acute Upper GI Bleeding?
quiz.stem: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 51 and ACG 2021 guidelines, what hemoglobin threshold is recommended for packed red blood cell transfusion in most hemodynamically stabilized patients with acute Upper GI Bleeding?
options: Hb < 11 g/dL
Hb < 10 g/dL
Hb < 7 g/dL (restrictive strategy)
Never transfuse regardless of hemoglobin
hints: Recall the landmark Villanueva NEJM trial cited in Ch. 51.
Over-transfusion increases portal venous pressure and precipitates variceal rebleeding!
Restrictive threshold Hb < 7 g/dL improves survival [Ref 22, 33].
quiz.rationale: A restrictive transfusion strategy (transfuse at Hb <7 g/dL, targeting 7–9 g/dL) significantly reduces rebleeding and mortality compared with liberal transfusion (<9 g/dL), especially in portal hypertension [Ref 22, 33].

quiz.text: At approximately what serum total bilirubin concentration does clinical scleral icterus (jaundice) typically become detectable on physical examination (Ch. 52)?
quiz.stem: At approximately what serum total bilirubin concentration does clinical scleral icterus (jaundice) typically become detectable on physical examination (Ch. 52)?
options: >= 0.8 mg/dL
>= 1.2 mg/dL
>= 3.0 mg/dL
hints: Normal total bilirubin is up to ~1.2 mg/dL, yet jaundice is not visible until higher.
Scleral elastin has high affinity for bilirubin.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 52 states scleral icterus becomes clinically evident at >=3.0 mg/dL.
quiz.rationale: Scleral icterus generally becomes detectable on exam when total serum bilirubin exceeds 3.0 mg/dL (differentiating true jaundice from carotenemia, which spares the sclera) [Ref 23].

quiz.text: A hospitalized cirrhotic patient with ascites develops mild fever and abdominal discomfort. Paracentesis shows ascitic fluid PMN count of 410 cells/uL (culture pending). What is the immediate action?
quiz.stem: A hospitalized cirrhotic patient with ascites develops mild fever and abdominal discomfort. Paracentesis shows ascitic fluid PMN count of 410 cells/uL (culture pending). What is the immediate action?
options: Wait 72 hours for culture sensitivity before giving antibiotics
Diagnose Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (PMN >=250/uL) and start IV Ceftriaxone (or Cefotaxime) + IV Albumin immediately
Give oral furosemide only
Repeat paracentesis in 1 week
hints: What is the diagnostic PMN threshold for SBP?
PMN >= 250 cells/uL confirms SBP immediately, even before cultures return!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 53 mandates immediate IV 3rd-generation cephalosporin + albumin.
quiz.rationale: Ascitic PMN >=250 cells/uL establishes SBP requiring immediate empiric IV third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime) plus IV albumin (1.5 g/kg Day 1, 1.0 g/kg Day 3) to prevent hepatorenal syndrome [Ref 24].

quiz.text: A 60-year-old cirrhotic patient presents with massive hematemesis. Alongside resuscitation and IV PPI, which TWO medications MUST be initiated immediately before upper endoscopy?
quiz.stem: A 60-year-old cirrhotic patient presents with massive hematemesis. Alongside resuscitation and IV PPI, which TWO medications MUST be initiated immediately before upper endoscopy?
options: IV Octreotide (vasoactive splanchnic vasoconstrictor) AND IV Ceftriaxone (prophylactic antibiotic)
Oral Beta-blocker (Propranolol) AND IV Heparin
IV Ketorolac AND Oral Lactulose alone
IV Furosemide AND Oral Aspirin
hints: In cirrhotic variceal bleeding, one drug lowers portal pressure and one prevents lethal bacterial infections/SBP.
Propranolol is for SECONDARY prophylaxis after stabilization — NEVER during active hemorrhagic shock!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 51 mandates IV Octreotide + IV Ceftriaxone immediately.
quiz.rationale: In suspected variceal bleeding, immediate IV octreotide (reduces portal pressure) and IV ceftriaxone (reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding, and mortality) must precede endoscopy [Ref 22].

quiz.text: What is the FIRST-LINE imaging study in a patient presenting with painless conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and markedly elevated Alkaline Phosphatase (480 U/L) & GGT?
quiz.stem: What is the FIRST-LINE imaging study in a patient presenting with painless conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and markedly elevated Alkaline Phosphatase (480 U/L) & GGT?
options: Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ) Abdominal Ultrasound to assess for intrahepatic/extrahepatic biliary ductal dilation
Immediate liver biopsy
Upper GI barium swallow
Serum ceruloplasmin alone
hints: First separate extrahepatic mechanical obstruction from intrahepatic cholestasis!
Which fast, radiation-free test visualizes dilated bile ducts and gallstones?
RUQ Ultrasound is the mandatory initial imaging test in cholestatic jaundice [Ch. 52].
quiz.rationale: In cholestatic jaundice (elevated ALP/GGT + direct bilirubin), RUQ ultrasound is the essential first imaging test to distinguish extrahepatic biliary obstruction (dilated ducts -> ERCP/MRCP) from intrahepatic cholestasis [Ref 23].

quiz.text: A 24-year-old medical student notices mild yellowing of his eyes during final exams after skipping meals. Labs show Total Bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL, Direct Bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL, normal AST/ALT/ALP, normal Hb, and normal reticulocyte count. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.stem: A 24-year-old medical student notices mild yellowing of his eyes during final exams after skipping meals. Labs show Total Bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL, Direct Bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL, normal AST/ALT/ALP, normal Hb, and normal reticulocyte count. What is the diagnosis?
options: Gilbert's syndrome (benign reduced UGT1A1 glucuronidation)
Acute viral hepatitis A
Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma
Primary biliary cholangitis
hints: Isolated indirect hyperbilirubinemia triggered by fasting/stress with normal CBC/retics (no hemolysis) and normal liver enzymes!
This affects ~5–8% of the general population.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 52 highlights Gilbert's syndrome requiring reassurance only.
quiz.rationale: Isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (<4 mg/dL) provoked by fasting/stress/illness with normal hemolysis markers and normal transaminases is classic Gilbert's syndrome (benign UGT1A1 promoter variant) [Ref 23].

quiz.text: Paracentesis shows Serum Albumin 3.4 g/dL, Ascitic Albumin 1.8 g/dL (SAAG 1.6 g/dL), AND Ascitic Total Protein 3.2 g/dL (>=2.5 g/dL). Which etiology best explains this High-SAAG, High-Protein ascites?
quiz.stem: Paracentesis shows Serum Albumin 3.4 g/dL, Ascitic Albumin 1.8 g/dL (SAAG 1.6 g/dL), AND Ascitic Total Protein 3.2 g/dL (>=2.5 g/dL). Which etiology best explains this High-SAAG, High-Protein ascites?
options: Cardiac ascites (Right Heart Failure / Constrictive Pericarditis)
Uncomplicated hepatic cirrhosis
Peritoneal carcinomatosis
Tuberculous peritonitis
hints: SAAG = 3.4 − 1.8 = 1.6 g/dL (>=1.1 = Portal Hypertension).
Now check Ascitic Total Protein: Cirrhosis has LOW protein (<2.5) due to capillarized sinusoids; Heart Failure has HIGH protein (>=2.5) because sinusoids remain intact!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 53 uses SAAG + Ascitic Total Protein to separate cardiac vs cirrhotic ascites.
quiz.rationale: SAAG >=1.1 g/dL confirms portal hypertension, and ascitic total protein >=2.5 g/dL distinguishes cardiac ascites (intact hepatic sinusoids leaking protein-rich lymph) from cirrhosis (protein <2.5 g/dL) [Ref 24].

quiz.text: A patient taking low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention of a prior coronary stent develops a bleeding peptic ulcer successfully treated with endoscopic hemostasis. According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 51, what should be done with the aspirin?
quiz.stem: A patient taking low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention of a prior coronary stent develops a bleeding peptic ulcer successfully treated with endoscopic hemostasis. According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 51, what should be done with the aspirin?
options: Permanently discontinue aspirin forever
Continue (or resume promptly within 1–3 days once hemostasis is achieved) alongside daily PPI therapy to prevent fatal cardiovascular thrombosis
Switch aspirin to high-dose ibuprofen
Hold aspirin for 6 months
hints: Compare mortality from recurrent ulcer bleed vs acute coronary stent thrombosis!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 51 explicitly notes patients on low-dose aspirin for secondary CV prevention should NOT permanently discontinue it.
Resume rapidly with PPI gastroprotection [Ref 22, 33].
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 51 [Ref 22] emphasizes that patients taking low-dose aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention should continue or promptly resume aspirin once endoscopic hemostasis is achieved (with PPI therapy), as withholding it markedly increases cardiovascular death.

quiz.text: Which ratio of Serum AST:ALT (>2:1 with absolute AST typically <300–500 U/L) classically points toward Alcoholic Hepatitis rather than ischemic or acute viral hepatitis?
quiz.stem: Which ratio of Serum AST:ALT (>2:1 with absolute AST typically <300–500 U/L) classically points toward Alcoholic Hepatitis rather than ischemic or acute viral hepatitis?
options: AST:ALT >= 2:1 with AST rarely exceeding 300–500 U/L (due to pyridoxal-5'-phosphate/B6 deficiency impairing ALT synthesis)
ALT > 5,000 U/L with normal AST
Isolated ALP > 1,000 U/L with normal GGT
Bilirubin > 20 mg/dL with normal AST/ALT
hints: Why is ALT disproportionately lower than AST in alcohol-related liver injury?
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) depletion reduces ALT more than AST, and alcohol causes mitochondrial AST release.
Ischemic hepatitis ('shock liver') and acetaminophen toxicity cause AST/ALT in the thousands (>1,000–5,000 U/L) [Ch. 52].
quiz.rationale: Alcoholic liver disease classically shows AST:ALT >=2:1 with AST rarely >300–500 U/L (reflecting mitochondrial injury and B6 depletion), whereas ischemic, viral, or acetaminophen injury produces transaminases >1,000 U/L [Ref 23].

quiz.text: Which bedside physical examination maneuver has the highest sensitivity for detecting moderate free ascitic fluid (~1.5 L) before paracentesis (Ch. 53)?
quiz.stem: Which bedside physical examination maneuver has the highest sensitivity for detecting moderate free ascitic fluid (~1.5 L) before paracentesis (Ch. 53)?
options: Flank dullness and Shifting Dullness (absent flank dullness makes ascites <10% likely)
Murphy's sign
Rovsing's sign
Tinel's sign
hints: Think about how free peritoneal fluid pools to the flanks when supine and shifts when turning lateral!
Fluid wave is specific but insensitive; flank/shifting dullness is the primary bedside screen.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 53 recommends flank/shifting dullness confirmed by bedside ultrasound [Ref 24].
quiz.rationale: Flank dullness and shifting dullness are the most sensitive bedside exam signs of ascites (absence of flank dullness strongly argues against significant ascites), with ultrasound confirming small volumes [Ref 24].

points.title: Upper vs Lower GI Bleeding Clinical Clues [Ref 22]
points.body: **Hematemesis** or **melena** (black tarry stool) localizes bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz (UGIB: peptic ulcer #1, varices, Mallory-Weiss, esophagitis). **Elevated BUN:Creatinine ratio (>20–30:1)** supports UGIB due to intestinal absorption of digested blood proteins. Remember: **brisk hematochezia with hemodynamic instability** can represent a massive UGIB (10–15% of severe hematochezia)!

points.title: SAAG + Total Protein Diagnostic Matrix (Ch. 53) [Ref 24]
rows: Cirrhosis, late Budd-Chiari, massive liver metastases
Heart failure (cardiac ascites), constrictive pericarditis, early Budd-Chiari

points.title: Glasgow-Blatchford Score & Severe Tropical Jaundice Mimics [Ref 22, 23]
points.body: A **Glasgow-Blatchford Score of 0–1** identifies very low-risk UGIB patients safe for outpatient management. In tropical/Indian settings, Harrison's 22e Ch. 52 reminds clinicians that **severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria** and **Weil's disease (leptospirosis)** produce combined jaundice + renal failure + fever/myalgias.

units.title: Fluid, Electrolyte & Acid-Base Fundamentals
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 56 & 58 — Hyponatremia ODS Limits, Hyperkalemia Triad, Winter's Formula & Corrected AG

points.title: Hyponatremia Golden Safety Law: Preventing Osmotic Demyelination [Ref 26]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 56 (Mount) [Ref 26]:** Overly rapid correction of chronic (>48h) hyponatremia (**>8–10 mEq/L in 24h** or **>18 mEq/L in 48h**) causes astrocyte/oligodendrocyte injury and catastrophic **Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (ODS)** (quadriparesis, locked-in syndrome). In high-risk patients (alcoholism, malnutrition, cirrhosis, hypokalemia), cap rise at **4–6 mEq/L in 24h**! For **seizures/coma**, give **100 mL 3% Hypertonic Saline IV over 10 min** to rapidly raise Na⁺ by 4–6 mEq/L.

points.title: Emergency Hyperkalemia Triad (K⁺ >6.5 or ANY ECG Change) [Ref 26]
rows: IV Calcium Gluconate 10% (10 mL = 1 g over 2–3 min)
Antagonizes membrane excitability; does NOT lower serum K⁺
IV Regular Insulin (5–10 U) + D50W (25–50g) + Nebulized Albuterol
Activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase -> drops K⁺ by 0.5–1.2 mEq/L (watch glucose!)
IV Loop Diuretic (if making urine), GI K⁺ Binder (SZC/Patiromer), or Dialysis
Removes total body potassium; definitive cure

points.title: 4-Step Systematic ABG Analysis (Ch. 58) [Ref 27]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 58 (DuBose) [Ref 27]**: **(1)** Inspect pH (<7.35 acidemia vs >7.45 alkalemia), PaCO₂, and HCO₃⁻. **(2)** In metabolic acidosis, apply **Winter's Equation: Expected PaCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2**. **(3)** Calculate **Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap = [Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)] + 2.5 × (4.0 − Albumin)**. **(4)** If HAGMA (>12), check **Delta-Delta (ΔAG / ΔHCO₃⁻)** to uncover hidden mixed disorders!

quiz.text: A patient with CKD presents with serum K+ 7.3 mEq/L and an ECG showing tall peaked T waves, absent P waves, and QRS widening (152 ms). What is the VERY FIRST drug to administer IV?
quiz.stem: A patient with CKD presents with serum K+ 7.3 mEq/L and an ECG showing tall peaked T waves, absent P waves, and QRS widening (152 ms). What is the VERY FIRST drug to administer IV?
options: Oral sodium zirconium cyclosilicate
IV Calcium Gluconate 10% (10 mL = 1 g over 2–3 min) to stabilize the cardiac membrane
IV Furosemide alone
IV Normal Saline 1 liter
hints: Which drug protects against imminent ventricular fibrillation in 1–3 minutes?
Calcium stabilizes the cardiac threshold potential immediately, even though it does not lower serum K+.
Always give IV Calcium FIRST when hyperkalemic ECG changes are present [Ch. 56].
quiz.rationale: Widened QRS in hyperkalemia predicts imminent sine-wave arrest; IV Calcium Gluconate 10% (1 g) must be pushed immediately to stabilize the myocardium within 1–3 minutes, followed by Insulin+Dextrose [Ref 26].

quiz.text: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 56 (Mount), exceeding what 24-hour sodium correction rate in chronic hyponatremia causes Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (ODS)?
quiz.stem: According to Harrison's 22e Ch. 56 (Mount), exceeding what 24-hour sodium correction rate in chronic hyponatremia causes Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (ODS)?
options: > 2 mEq/L in 24 hours
> 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours (or >18 mEq/L in 48 hours; limit to 4–6 mEq/L in high-risk alcoholism/malnutrition/cirrhosis)
> 25 mEq/L in 24 hours
Sodium correction rate does not affect the brain
hints: Recall the exact Harrison's 22e Ch. 56 ODS correction limit.
Maximum 8–10 mEq/L in 24h (and 4–6 mEq/L if malnourished/alcoholic/cirrhotic).
Never exceed 18 mEq/L in 48h [Ref 26].
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 56 [Ref 26] specifies that raising serum Na+ faster than 8–10 mEq/L in 24h (or 18 mEq/L in 48h) induces astrocytic hypertonic stress and oligodendrocyte loss (ODS).

quiz.text: A patient with chronic hyponatremia (Na+ 112 mEq/L) suddenly develops a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the ED. What is the immediate life-saving treatment?
quiz.stem: A patient with chronic hyponatremia (Na+ 112 mEq/L) suddenly develops a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the ED. What is the immediate life-saving treatment?
options: Fluid restriction to 1 liter/day and recheck tomorrow
100 mL IV bolus of 3% Hypertonic Saline over 10 minutes (repeating if seizures persist) to rapidly raise Na+ by 4–6 mEq/L
Oral salt tablets alone
IV 5% Dextrose in Water (D5W)
hints: Seizures/coma from hyponatremia mean acute cerebral edema and imminent herniation!
A controlled 4–6 mEq/L immediate bump with 100 mL 3% NaCl stops seizures safely while staying within the 24h ODS ceiling.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 56 recommends 100 mL 3% NaCl boluses for severe CNS symptoms.
quiz.rationale: Severely symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures/coma) requires immediate 100 mL IV boluses of 3% hypertonic saline over 10 minutes to achieve a rapid 4–6 mEq/L increase that reverses cerebral edema [Ref 26].

quiz.text: A patient with severe hyperkalemia receives 10 units IV Regular Insulin + 25 g IV Dextrose. What mandatory bedside monitoring must nursing perform over the next 4–6 hours?
quiz.stem: A patient with severe hyperkalemia receives 10 units IV Regular Insulin + 25 g IV Dextrose. What mandatory bedside monitoring must nursing perform over the next 4–6 hours?
options: Hourly capillary blood glucose checks because delayed severe hypoglycemia is common (especially in CKD)
Only check blood pressure once at discharge
Check serum amylase every 15 minutes
No monitoring needed after 30 minutes
hints: Insulin stays active far longer than the initial IV dextrose bolus, especially when renal insulin clearance is impaired!
Iatrogenic hypoglycemia is the #1 preventable complication of hyperkalemia therapy.
Check fingerstick glucose hourly for 4–6 hours [Ch. 56].
quiz.rationale: Because insulin half-life is prolonged in renal failure while IV dextrose is rapidly metabolized, hourly point-of-care glucose checks for 4–6 hours are mandatory to prevent delayed hypoglycemia [Ref 26].

quiz.text: A septic patient has Na+ 138, Cl- 104, HCO3- 16 mEq/L, and serum Albumin 2.0 g/dL. What is the ALBUMIN-CORRECTED Anion Gap (Ch. 58)?
quiz.stem: A septic patient has Na+ 138, Cl- 104, HCO3- 16 mEq/L, and serum Albumin 2.0 g/dL. What is the ALBUMIN-CORRECTED Anion Gap (Ch. 58)?
options: 18 mEq/L
23 mEq/L
13 mEq/L
10 mEq/L
hints: First compute Raw AG = 138 − (104 + 16) = 18.
Next apply albumin correction: +2.5 mEq/L for every 1.0 g/dL albumin below 4.0.
quiz.rationale: Raw AG = 138 − 120 = 18. Because albumin is 2.0 g/dL below 4.0, add 2.5 × 2.0 = +5 -> Corrected AG = 23 mEq/L. Failing to adjust for hypoalbuminemia frequently hides a severe lactic acidosis [Ref 27].

quiz.text: Using Winter's Formula [PaCO2 = (1.5 × HCO3-) + 8 ± 2], a patient with DKA has pH 7.16, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, and measured PaCO2 34 mmHg. What is the complete acid-base diagnosis?
quiz.stem: Using Winter's Formula [PaCO2 = (1.5 × HCO3-) + 8 ± 2], a patient with DKA has pH 7.16, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, and measured PaCO2 34 mmHg. What is the complete acid-base diagnosis?
options: Simple compensated metabolic acidosis
Primary Metabolic Acidosis PLUS concurrent Primary Respiratory Acidosis (impending ventilatory fatigue!)
Primary Metabolic Acidosis PLUS concurrent Respiratory Alkalosis
Pure Respiratory Alkalosis
hints: Plug HCO3- = 10 into Winter's equation: (1.5 × 10) + 8 ± 2.
Expected PaCO2 = 23 ± 2 (21–25 mmHg).
Measured PaCO2 is 34 mmHg (HIGHER than expected) = CO2 retention / superimposed Respiratory Acidosis!
quiz.rationale: Expected PaCO2 = (1.5 × 10) + 8 ± 2 = 21–25 mmHg. A measured PaCO2 of 34 mmHg is inappropriately high, signifying a superimposed Respiratory Acidosis (often warning of respiratory muscle exhaustion) [Ref 27].

quiz.text: A diabetic patient presents in DKA with Glucose 600 mg/dL and measured serum Na+ 128 mEq/L. Approximately what is the glucose-corrected serum Na+ (Ch. 56)?
quiz.stem: A diabetic patient presents in DKA with Glucose 600 mg/dL and measured serum Na+ 128 mEq/L. Approximately what is the glucose-corrected serum Na+ (Ch. 56)?
options: 128 mEq/L (no correction needed)
136 to 140 mEq/L (hypertonic translocational hyponatremia)
118 mEq/L
152 mEq/L
hints: Hyperglycemia pulls water out of cells, diluting extracellular Na+.
Add ~1.6 mEq/L (up to 2.4 mEq/L at glucose >400) for every 100 mg/dL glucose above 100.
500 mg/dL excess -> +8 to +12 mEq/L -> Corrected Na+ ≈ 136–140 mEq/L [Ch. 56].
quiz.rationale: Glucose is an effective osmole that shifts water out of cells; correcting by +1.6 to 2.4 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL glucose >100 yields a normal corrected Na+ (136–140 mEq/L), avoiding inappropriate hypertonic saline [Ref 26].

quiz.text: A patient presents with tinnitus, fever, hyperventilation, pH 7.42, PaCO2 22 mmHg, HCO3- 14 mEq/L, and Corrected Anion Gap 22 mEq/L. What classic intoxication produces this exact mixed acid-base pattern?
quiz.stem: A patient presents with tinnitus, fever, hyperventilation, pH 7.42, PaCO2 22 mmHg, HCO3- 14 mEq/L, and Corrected Anion Gap 22 mEq/L. What classic intoxication produces this exact mixed acid-base pattern?
options: Salicylate (Aspirin) toxicity — Primary Respiratory Alkalosis + High-Anion-Gap Metabolic Acidosis
Opioid overdose
Ethylene glycol ingestion alone
Loop diuretic abuse
hints: Notice the NORMAL pH (7.42) despite severely abnormal PaCO2 (22) AND HCO3- (14) AND AG (22)!
Salicylates directly stimulate the medullary respiratory center AND uncouple oxidative phosphorylation.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 58 highlights salicylates as the classic mixed HAGMA + Respiratory Alkalosis.
quiz.rationale: Salicylate toxicity directly stimulates medullary respiration (primary respiratory alkalosis) while impairing mitochondrial metabolism (HAGMA), often producing a near-normal pH with low PaCO2, low HCO3-, and high AG [Ref 27].

quiz.text: In severe Metabolic Alkalosis, how does a spot Urine Chloride (UCl-) differentiate Saline-Responsive from Saline-Resistant causes (Ch. 58)?
quiz.stem: In severe Metabolic Alkalosis, how does a spot Urine Chloride (UCl-) differentiate Saline-Responsive from Saline-Resistant causes (Ch. 58)?
options: Urine Cl- < 20 mEq/L = Saline-Responsive (vomiting, NG suction, prior diuretics -> treat with 0.9% NaCl + KCl); Urine Cl- > 20 mEq/L = Saline-Resistant (hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's, Bartter/Gitelman)
Urine Cl- > 100 mEq/L = Vomiting
Urine Cl- is always zero in alkalosis
Urine Cl- only measures renal failure
hints: Volume/chloride depletion makes the kidneys avidly retain Cl- (UCl- <20).
Excess mineralocorticoid activity causes volume expansion and renal Cl- wasting (UCl- >20).
Harrison's 22e Ch. 58 uses UCl- (<20 vs >20) as the key branch point in metabolic alkalosis.
quiz.rationale: Low urine chloride (<20 mEq/L) reflects volume/chloride depletion (vomiting, NG suction) responsive to 0.9% NaCl + KCl; high urine chloride (>20 mEq/L) indicates mineralocorticoid excess, active diuretics, or Bartter/Gitelman syndromes [Ref 27].

quiz.text: A patient with SIADH has Na+ 122 mEq/L and Urine Osmolality 620 mOsm/kg. Why can infusing 1 liter of 0.9% Normal Saline (308 mOsm/L) paradoxically WORSEN their hyponatremia?
quiz.stem: A patient with SIADH has Na+ 122 mEq/L and Urine Osmolality 620 mOsm/kg. Why can infusing 1 liter of 0.9% Normal Saline (308 mOsm/L) paradoxically WORSEN their hyponatremia?
options: Because the kidneys excrete the NaCl load in a smaller volume of hypertonic urine (620 mOsm/kg) and RETAIN free water ('desalination phenomenon')
Because 0.9% NaCl contains no sodium
Because Normal Saline causes immediate potassium arrest
Because SIADH inhibits all urine output
hints: Compare the osmolality of infused fluid (308 mOsm/L) to the fixed concentrated urine (620 mOsm/kg)!
1 L of 0.9% NaCl provides 308 mOsm -> excreted in only 0.5 L of urine -> net +0.5 L free water retained!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 56 warns against 0.9% NaCl when Urine Osm > 2× Plasma Osm in SIADH.
quiz.rationale: In SIADH with fixed high urine osmolality (e.g., 620 mOsm/kg), the 308 mOsm of solute in 1 L of 0.9% NaCl is excreted in only ~0.5 L of urine, leaving ~0.5 L of free water behind and further lowering serum Na+ [Ref 26].

points.title: High-Anion-Gap Metabolic Acidosis Mnemonic: GOLDMARK [Ref 27]
points.body: **G**lycols (ethylene/propylene glycol), **O**xoproline (5-oxoproline / chronic acetaminophen in malnourished), **L**-Lactate (sepsis, shock, ischemia), **D**-Lactate (short bowel), **M**ethanol, **A**spirin (salicylates), **R**enal failure (uremia), **K**etoacidosis (DKA, alcoholic, starvation).

points.title: Hypernatremia Free Water Deficit Formula [Ref 26]
points.body: **Free Water Deficit = TBW × [(Serum Na⁺ / 140) − 1]**, where Total Body Water (TBW) ≈ **0.6 × wt(kg)** in men and **0.5 × wt(kg)** in women/elderly. Just like hyponatremia, correct **chronic hypernatremia slowly (<=10 mEq/L per 24h)** to avoid rebound cerebral edema!

points.title: Osmolar Gap & Desmopressin (DDAVP) Clamp for Overcorrection [Ref 26, 27]
points.body: An **Osmolar Gap >10 mOsm/kg** (Measured Osm − [2×Na + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8]) indicates unmeasured toxic alcohols (**methanol, ethylene glycol** -> immediate **fomepizole**). If hyponatremia begins auto-correcting too rapidly (>6–8 mEq/L/24h via water diuresis), immediately administer **IV Desmopressin (DDAVP 1–2 mcg)** + **D5W** to re-lower Na⁺ and avert ODS!

units.title: Approach to Azotemia, Anemia & Bleeding/Thrombosis
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 55, 66 & 69 — Prerenal vs ATN, Urine Casts, Reticulocyte Index & Coagulopathy

points.title: Acute Kidney Injury (Azotemia): Prerenal vs Intrinsic vs Postrenal [Ref 25, 34]
rows: Muddy brown granular casts & renal tubular epithelial cells
Supportive perfusion, stop nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, vancomycin)
GN: Dysmorphic RBCs & RBC casts | AIN: WBC casts
Urgent serologies/nephrology; stop culprit drug (beta-lactams/PPI/NSAID) in AIN
Immediate bedside bladder ultrasound / Foley catheter!

points.title: Kinetic & Morphologic Classification of Anemia [Ref 28]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 66 (DeLoughery & Longo) [Ref 28]**, always pair the **Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI)** with **MCV**: **RPI < 2** = marrow hypoproliferation (iron/B12/folate deficiency, CKD, marrow failure); **RPI >= 2.5** = appropriate marrow response to **hemolysis** or **acute blood loss**. Microcytic (**MCV <80**): Iron deficiency (low ferritin, high TIBC), Thalassemia (normal/high RBC count, low Mentzer), Anemia of Chronic Disease, Sideroblastic. Macrocytic (**MCV >100**): B12/Folate (hypersegmented neutrophils), Alcohol, Liver disease, Hypothyroidism, MDS.

points.title: Primary vs Secondary Hemostasis & Coagulation Mixing Study [Ref 29]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 69 (Konkle) [Ref 29]:** **Primary hemostasis defects** (platelets/vWF) cause immediate **mucocutaneous bleeding** (petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, menorrhagia). **Secondary coagulation factor defects** (Hemophilia A/B, vitamin K deficiency) cause **delayed deep bleeding** (hemarthroses, retroperitoneal/muscle hematomas). A **1:1 Mixing Study** separates **Factor Deficiency** (PT/aPTT **CORRECTS**) from a **Factor Inhibitor** (e.g., lupus anticoagulant or acquired Factor VIII antibody -> **FAILS to correct**).

quiz.text: Which urine microscopy finding is pathognomonic for Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) rather than Prerenal Azotemia (Ch. 55)?
quiz.stem: Which urine microscopy finding is pathognomonic for Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) rather than Prerenal Azotemia (Ch. 55)?
options: Hyaline casts only
Muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells
Red blood cell casts with dysmorphic RBCs
Calcium oxalate crystals only
hints: Hyaline casts = prerenal; RBC casts = glomerulonephritis; WBC casts = pyelonephritis/AIN.
Necrotic sloughed tubular cells clump into 'muddy brown' casts.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 55 highlights muddy brown granular casts + FENa >2% as classic ATN.
quiz.rationale: Muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells (typically paired with FENa >2%) establish ischemic or nephrotoxic Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) [Ref 25].

quiz.text: An elderly man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presents with acute rise in serum creatinine from 1.0 to 4.2 mg/dL and suprapubic fullness. What is the single fastest first-line diagnostic and therapeutic step?
quiz.stem: An elderly man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presents with acute rise in serum creatinine from 1.0 to 4.2 mg/dL and suprapubic fullness. What is the single fastest first-line diagnostic and therapeutic step?
options: Perform a kidney biopsy immediately
Bedside bladder ultrasound (post-void residual) and urinary catheter (Foley) placement to relieve postrenal obstruction
Start high-dose IV corticosteroids
Administer IV contrast CT abdomen
hints: Always rule out easily reversible POSTRENAL obstruction early in AKI!
Bladder scan takes 30 seconds and avoids nephrotoxic contrast.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 55 & KDIGO emphasize early ultrasound exclusion of obstruction.
quiz.rationale: Postrenal obstruction is rapidly reversible; immediate bedside bladder scan/renal ultrasound and Foley decompression prevent permanent nephron loss without nephrotoxic contrast [Ref 25, 34].

quiz.text: A young woman presents with recurrent epistaxis, gum bleeding, heavy menstrual periods, and pinpoint petechiae on her shins (normal PT and aPTT). Which arm of hemostasis is impaired?
quiz.stem: A young woman presents with recurrent epistaxis, gum bleeding, heavy menstrual periods, and pinpoint petechiae on her shins (normal PT and aPTT). Which arm of hemostasis is impaired?
options: Primary hemostasis (platelets or von Willebrand factor)
Secondary hemostasis (intrinsic coagulation cascade Factors VIII/IX)
Fibrinolysis only
Antithrombin III deficiency
hints: Petechiae + mucocutaneous bleeding + normal PT/aPTT!
Deep joint bleeds = secondary factors; superficial mucocutaneous/petechial bleeds = platelets/vWF.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 69 contrasts mucocutaneous primary bleeding vs deep secondary bleeding.
quiz.rationale: Petechiae and mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia) with normal PT/aPTT indicate a primary hemostasis disorder (thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, or vWD) [Ref 29].

quiz.text: Which single laboratory test is the MOST specific indicator of depleted body iron stores in uncomplicated microcytic anemia (Ch. 66)?
quiz.stem: Which single laboratory test is the MOST specific indicator of depleted body iron stores in uncomplicated microcytic anemia (Ch. 66)?
options: Low Serum Ferritin (<15–30 ng/mL)
Elevated Serum B12
Elevated Reticulocyte Count
Low Serum Creatinine
hints: Ferritin reflects storage iron directly.
Note that ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, so a LOW ferritin is virtually diagnostic of iron deficiency.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 66 defines low ferritin + high TIBC + low transferrin saturation as iron deficiency anemia.
quiz.rationale: A low serum ferritin (<15–30 ng/mL) is the most specific marker of depleted iron stores; remember that inflammation can falsely elevate ferritin into the normal range [Ref 28].

quiz.text: A patient taking daily furosemide develops volume-depleted prerenal AKI. Why is Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa) unreliable here, and which test should be used instead?
quiz.stem: A patient taking daily furosemide develops volume-depleted prerenal AKI. Why is Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa) unreliable here, and which test should be used instead?
options: Loop diuretics force urinary sodium excretion (falsely raising FENa >1%); use Fractional Excretion of Urea (FEUrea <35% favors prerenal)
Furosemide lowers serum creatinine artificially
FENa only works in children
Use serum amylase instead
hints: Diuretics block Na+ reabsorption in the loop of Henle, making urine Na+ high even when dehydrated!
Urea reabsorption in the proximal tubule is NOT blocked by loop/thiazide diuretics.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 55 recommends FEUrea (<35% = prerenal) when patients are on diuretics.
quiz.rationale: Diuretics increase urinary Na+ excretion and falsely elevate FENa above 1%; FEUrea (<35%) remains reliable for identifying prerenal physiology during diuretic use [Ref 25].

quiz.text: A 65-year-old man presents with macrocytic anemia (Hb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 116 fL), hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear, glossitis, and loss of vibration/proprioception in his feet. What is the diagnosis and critical therapeutic warning?
quiz.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with macrocytic anemia (Hb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 116 fL), hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear, glossitis, and loss of vibration/proprioception in his feet. What is the diagnosis and critical therapeutic warning?
options: Vitamin B12 deficiency — NEVER treat with Folate monotherapy alone, because Folate corrects the anemia while allowing irreversible subacute combined spinal cord degeneration to worsen!
Iron deficiency — give oral ferrous sulfate
Folate deficiency — give oral folic acid only
Thalassemia minor — reassure only
hints: Macrocytic anemia + hypersegmented neutrophils + dorsal column/neurologic deficits = B12 (NOT folate)!
Folate can mask the hematologic picture while spinal cord demyelination progresses.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 66 underscores checking B12 and methylmalonic acid before isolated folate therapy.
quiz.rationale: Both B12 and folate deficiency cause megaloblastic macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, but ONLY B12 deficiency causes neurologic deficits (dorsal column/corticospinal tract). Treating with folate alone worsens neurologic injury [Ref 28].

quiz.text: An isolated prolonged aPTT (68 sec; normal PT/INR) is evaluated with a 1:1 Mixing Study using normal pooled plasma. After mixing, the aPTT FAILS to correct (remains 64 sec). What does this prove?
quiz.stem: An isolated prolonged aPTT (68 sec; normal PT/INR) is evaluated with a 1:1 Mixing Study using normal pooled plasma. After mixing, the aPTT FAILS to correct (remains 64 sec). What does this prove?
options: Presence of a circulating coagulation INHIBITOR (e.g., lupus anticoagulant or acquired Factor VIII antibody)
Simple Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency)
Simple Vitamin K deficiency
Laboratory dilution error
hints: Normal plasma supplies >50% of every clotting factor, which is plenty to normalize a deficiency.
If adding 50% normal factors STILL fails to normalize aPTT, something in the patient's plasma is actively INHIBITING clotting!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 69: Correction = Deficiency; Non-correction = Inhibitor.
quiz.rationale: Failure of a 1:1 mixing study to normalize a prolonged aPTT confirms a circulating inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant—which paradoxically causes thrombosis—or an acquired factor VIII inhibitor causing severe bleeding) [Ref 29].

quiz.text: A septic ICU patient develops oozing from IV sites with platelets 42,000/uL, prolonged PT AND aPTT, markedly elevated D-dimer, LOW fibrinogen (<100 mg/dL), and schistocytes on smear. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.stem: A septic ICU patient develops oozing from IV sites with platelets 42,000/uL, prolonged PT AND aPTT, markedly elevated D-dimer, LOW fibrinogen (<100 mg/dL), and schistocytes on smear. What is the diagnosis?
options: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP — normal PT/aPTT/fibrinogen)
Hemophilia A
hints: Look closely at PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, AND D-dimer!
In TTP/HUS, platelets drop and schistocytes appear, but PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen remain NORMAL.
Consumptive coagulopathy (high PT/aPTT + low fibrinogen + high D-dimer + low platelets) = DIC [Ch. 69].
quiz.rationale: DIC causes widespread microvascular thrombin consumption: thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and aPTT, hypofibrinogenemia, markedly elevated D-dimer, and microangiopathic schistocytes—distinguishing it from TTP/HUS (normal PT/aPTT) [Ref 29].

quiz.text: A patient presents with Hb 7.8 g/dL, MCV 94 fL, Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI) 3.8, elevated indirect bilirubin, high LDH, undetectable haptoglobin (<8 mg/dL), and spherocytes on peripheral smear. What is the mechanism?
quiz.stem: A patient presents with Hb 7.8 g/dL, MCV 94 fL, Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI) 3.8, elevated indirect bilirubin, high LDH, undetectable haptoglobin (<8 mg/dL), and spherocytes on peripheral smear. What is the mechanism?
options: Hemolytic anemia (appropriate marrow hyperproliferation, RPI >=2.5) — check Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test for Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
Aplastic anemia (marrow failure)
Anemia of Chronic Kidney Disease
Iron deficiency anemia
hints: RPI 3.8 (>=2.5) means the bone marrow is working overtime!
High LDH + high indirect bilirubin + undetectable haptoglobin = RBC destruction (hemolysis).
Spherocytes -> evaluate for warm AIHA (DAT positive) vs hereditary spherocytosis [Ch. 66].
quiz.rationale: RPI >=2.5 confirms marrow hyperproliferation; combined with elevated LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, depleted haptoglobin, and spherocytes, this defines hemolytic anemia (order DAT/Coombs to rule in AIHA) [Ref 28].

quiz.text: Under KDIGO criteria cited in Harrison's 22e Ch. 55, what minimum acute rise in serum creatinine establishes Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)?
quiz.stem: Under KDIGO criteria cited in Harrison's 22e Ch. 55, what minimum acute rise in serum creatinine establishes Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)?
options: Rise >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, OR >= 1.5× baseline within 7 days, OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
Rise >= 3.0 mg/dL within 24 hours only
Any serum creatinine > 1.0 mg/dL regardless of baseline
Urine output < 2 liters/day
hints: Remember how small an absolute creatinine jump signals significant GFR loss!
Because Cr vs GFR is hyperbolic, a tiny 0.3 mg/dL jump from 0.8 to 1.1 reflects a major GFR drop.
KDIGO: >=0.3 mg/dL in 48h, >=1.5x baseline in 7d, or UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h x 6h [Ref 25, 34].
quiz.rationale: KDIGO defines AKI by a serum creatinine increase >=0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, >=1.5× baseline within 7 days, or oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h for >=6 hours [Ref 25, 34].

points.title: Iron Studies Differential Matrix (Ch. 66) [Ref 28]
rows: Microcytic, hypochromic, high RDW, pencil cells
Normocytic -> microcytic; hepcidin traps iron in macrophages
Microcytic with normal/high RBC count, target cells, Mentzer <13

points.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) & TTP Emergency Recognition [Ref 29]
points.body: **HIT (4Ts score)**: >50% platelet drop 5–10 days after heparin with **paradoxical THROMBOSIS** -> stop ALL heparin immediately and start non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban/bivalirudin/fondaparinux; NEVER give warfarin until platelets >150k!). **TTP (PLASMIC score)**: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + normal PT/aPTT (ADAMTS13 <10%) -> emergent **plasma exchange** (avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening hemorrhage).

units.title: Principles of Clinical Pharmacology, Ethics & Palliative Care
units.subtitle: Harrison's 22e Ch. 71, 12 & 13 — Pharmacokinetics, Decision Capacity, Informed Consent & SPIKES

points.title: Core Pharmacokinetic Laws Every Clinician Must Master [Ref 30]
rows: Depends on Volume of Distribution — UNCHANGED in renal failure!
Depends on Clearance — MUST REDUCE in renal/hepatic failure!
Time for concentration to fall 50%; determines dosing interval
Independent of dose size! Doubling dose does NOT reach steady state faster

points.title: The 4 Pillars of Biomedical Ethics & Decision-Making Capacity [Ref 8]
points.body: **Harrison's 22e Ch. 12 (Grady & Lo) [Ref 8]:** Clinical ethics balances **Autonomy**, **Beneficence**, **Nonmaleficence**, and **Justice**. **Decision-making capacity** is a clinical judgment specific to a single decision (NOT a court ruling of competence) assessed by 4 criteria: **(1) Understanding** relevant facts, **(2) Appreciation** of consequences to oneself, **(3) Reasoning** through options, and **(4) Communicating** a consistent choice. A patient with intact capacity may refuse even life-saving treatment!

points.title: Palliative Care & SPIKES Communication Protocol [Ref 9]
points.body: Per **Harrison's 22e Ch. 13 (Emanuel & Urwin) [Ref 9]**, **palliative care** is appropriate at **ANY stage of serious illness** alongside curative therapy—it is NOT restricted to the final weeks of life (hospice). Deliver serious news using **SPIKES**: **S**etting -> **P**erception -> **I**nvitation -> **K**nowledge (clear warning shot, no jargon) -> **E**motions (empathy) -> **S**trategy/Summary.

quiz.text: A 70-year-old patient with severe CKD (CrCl 22 mL/min) needs urgent IV Vancomycin for MRSA septic shock. How should you adjust the INITIAL LOADING DOSE vs the MAINTENANCE DOSE (Ch. 71)?
quiz.stem: A 70-year-old patient with severe CKD (CrCl 22 mL/min) needs urgent IV Vancomycin for MRSA septic shock. How should you adjust the INITIAL LOADING DOSE vs the MAINTENANCE DOSE (Ch. 71)?
options: Cut the loading dose by 75% and keep maintenance dose normal
Give a FULL weight-based Loading Dose (depends on Volume of Distribution), then REDUCE/EXTEND the Maintenance Dose interval (depends on renal clearance)
Give neither loading nor maintenance dose in CKD
Double the maintenance dose to clear the infection faster
hints: Recall the two pharmacokinetic equations: LD depends on Vd; MD depends on CL.
Renal failure lowers Clearance (CL), NOT Volume of Distribution (Vd)!
Cutting the loading dose causes subtherapeutic levels during the critical golden hours of sepsis [Ch. 71].
quiz.rationale: Loading dose depends on Volume of Distribution (LD = Vd × Ctarget / F) and remains unchanged in renal impairment; maintenance dose depends on Clearance (CL) and must be reduced or extended [Ref 30].

quiz.text: Approximately how many elimination half-lives (t½) are required for a drug administered at a constant maintenance schedule to reach steady-state plasma concentration (~94–97%)?
quiz.stem: Approximately how many elimination half-lives (t½) are required for a drug administered at a constant maintenance schedule to reach steady-state plasma concentration (~94–97%)?
options: 1 half-life
2 half-lives
4 to 5 half-lives
20 half-lives
hints: Notice this does NOT depend on dose size!
Harrison's 22e Ch. 71 establishes 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state.
quiz.rationale: Under first-order kinetics, a drug reaches ~94% of steady state after 4 half-lives and ~97% after 5 half-lives—regardless of dose magnitude (which changes the height of steady state, not the time to reach it) [Ref 30].

quiz.text: A 72-year-old man with advanced colon cancer demonstrates full understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and consistent communication of his choice to decline chemotherapy despite his family's objections. What is the ethically required action (Ch. 12)?
quiz.stem: A 72-year-old man with advanced colon cancer demonstrates full understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and consistent communication of his choice to decline chemotherapy despite his family's objections. What is the ethically required action (Ch. 12)?
options: Override his refusal because his family disagrees
Respect his autonomous refusal (providing full symptom & palliative support) because an adult with intact decision-making capacity has the right to refuse any medical intervention
Declare him incompetent simply because he disagreed with the physician
Administer chemotherapy secretly
hints: Disagreeing with a doctor does NOT mean a patient lacks capacity!
Autonomy grants capacitated adults the right to refuse even life-prolonging interventions.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 12 confirms informed refusal by a capacitated patient must be respected.
quiz.rationale: Respect for autonomy mandates honoring informed refusal of treatment by any adult with intact decision-making capacity (understanding, appreciation, reasoning, communicating a choice), while continuing compassionate supportive care [Ref 8].

quiz.text: Which statement accurately differentiates PALLIATIVE CARE from HOSPICE CARE in Harrison's 22e Ch. 13?
quiz.stem: Which statement accurately differentiates PALLIATIVE CARE from HOSPICE CARE in Harrison's 22e Ch. 13?
options: Palliative care is appropriate at ANY stage of serious illness concurrently with curative/disease-directed therapy; hospice is a subset focused on comfort when prognosis is typically <=6 months and curative intent ceases
Palliative care can only start in the final 48 hours of life
Palliative care forbids administering antibiotics or chemotherapy
Palliative care and euthanasia are synonyms
hints: Does a patient with newly diagnosed metastatic lung cancer have to stop oncology treatment to receive palliative care?
No! Early concurrent palliative care improves BOTH quality of life AND survival (Temel NEJM trial).
Harrison's 22e Ch. 13 emphasizes early integration of palliative care alongside disease-modifying treatment.
quiz.rationale: Palliative care relieves physical, psychosocial, and spiritual suffering at any point in a serious illness alongside curative therapy, whereas hospice specifically serves patients near the end of life (typically <=6-month prognosis) focusing purely on comfort [Ref 9].

quiz.text: In the SPIKES protocol for delivering serious medical news (Ch. 13), what should the clinician do right after establishing the Setting ('S') and BEFORE delivering medical Knowledge ('K')?
quiz.stem: In the SPIKES protocol for delivering serious medical news (Ch. 13), what should the clinician do right after establishing the Setting ('S') and BEFORE delivering medical Knowledge ('K')?
options: Immediately list all 5-year survival statistics in technical jargon
Assess the patient's Perception ('P' — 'What have you been told so far?') and ask for their Invitation ('I' — how much detail they want)
Hand the patient a brochure and exit the room
Ask the family to leave without permission
hints: Before you tell, ASK!
Knowing what the patient already understands prevents blind-siding and aligns empathy.
S-P-I-K-E-S: Setting -> Perception -> Invitation -> Knowledge -> Emotions -> Strategy [Ref 9].
quiz.rationale: Assessing the patient's current Perception and obtaining an Invitation for how they wish to receive information ensures bad news is delivered with compassion, clarity, and alignment with the patient's readiness [Ref 9].

quiz.text: Why does Harrison's 22e Ch. 71 prefer the term medication 'ADHERENCE' over 'COMPLIANCE'?
quiz.stem: Why does Harrison's 22e Ch. 71 prefer the term medication 'ADHERENCE' over 'COMPLIANCE'?
options: Because 'adherence' reflects a collaborative partnership between patient and clinician and removes blaming language implying the patient is solely at fault
Because 'compliance' is a trademarked brand name
Because adherence only applies to IV medications
There is no difference between the two terms
hints: Look at our verified Ch. 71 Global Considerations excerpt!
'Compliance' implies passive obedience and blames the patient when barriers (cost, side effects, literacy) interfere.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 71 explicitly recommends 'adherence'.
quiz.rationale: Harrison's 22e Ch. 71 [Ref 30] states that 'adherence' is preferred over 'compliance' because it removes paternalistic blame and acknowledges shared decision-making plus cost/access barriers.

quiz.text: A patient stable on warfarin starts rifampin for tuberculosis. One week later, their INR drops from 2.5 to 1.1 and they develop a DVT. What pharmacokinetic interaction occurred?
quiz.stem: A patient stable on warfarin starts rifampin for tuberculosis. One week later, their INR drops from 2.5 to 1.1 and they develop a DVT. What pharmacokinetic interaction occurred?
options: Rifampin is a potent CYP450 enzyme INDUCER, accelerating hepatic metabolism of warfarin and lowering its plasma levels
Rifampin inhibits CYP450, causing warfarin toxicity
Rifampin blocks renal excretion of warfarin
Rifampin chelates vitamin K in the stomach
hints: Did warfarin activity go UP (inhibition) or DOWN (induction)?
INR fell to 1.1 -> warfarin was cleared much faster!
Rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and St. John's wort are classic potent CYP inducers [Ch. 71].
quiz.rationale: Rifampin strongly induces hepatic CYP2C9/3A4 enzymes, markedly accelerating warfarin clearance and causing subtherapeutic INR unless warfarin dose is closely monitored and increased [Ref 30].

quiz.text: A terminally ill patient with severe air hunger (refractory dyspnea) receives carefully titrated IV morphine for symptom relief, with the known foreseeable risk of modest respiratory slowing. Which ethical principle in Harrison's 22e Ch. 13 justifies this?
quiz.stem: A terminally ill patient with severe air hunger (refractory dyspnea) receives carefully titrated IV morphine for symptom relief, with the known foreseeable risk of modest respiratory slowing. Which ethical principle in Harrison's 22e Ch. 13 justifies this?
options: The Doctrine of Double Effect — the clinician's primary INTENT is relieving severe suffering, not hastening death, and the dose is proportionate to symptom relief
Paternalistic beneficence overriding patient wishes
Therapeutic privilege
Medical futility
hints: Distinguish intended effect (relieving unbearable dyspnea/pain) from foreseeable unintended side effect.
Properly titrated opioids for dyspnea rarely hasten death and are standard palliative care.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 12 & 13 anchor this under the Doctrine of Double Effect.
quiz.rationale: The ethical Doctrine of Double Effect permits proportionate opioid/sedative titration when the clinician's intent is purely relieving refractory pain or dyspnea, even if respiratory depression is a foreseeable secondary risk [Ref 8, 9].

quiz.text: When a patient lacks decision-making capacity and has NO written advance directive, how should a surrogate decision-maker determine what treatment to authorize (Ch. 12)?
quiz.stem: When a patient lacks decision-making capacity and has NO written advance directive, how should a surrogate decision-maker determine what treatment to authorize (Ch. 12)?
options: Apply 'Substituted Judgment' FIRST (what the patient themselves would have wanted based on their known values/prior statements), falling back to 'Best Interests' only if the patient's wishes are unknown
Do whatever the surrogate personally prefers for themselves
Always choose maximal life support regardless of patient values
Flip a coin among family members
hints: Whose values matter most in surrogate decision-making?
First reconstruct the patient's own authentic voice ('Substituted Judgment'); only if completely unknown use 'Best Interests'.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 12 outlines the strict hierarchy: Advance Directive -> Substituted Judgment -> Best Interests.
quiz.rationale: Surrogate decision-making follows a strict ethical hierarchy: (1) Written Advance Directive -> (2) Substituted Judgment (enacting what the patient would have chosen) -> (3) Best Interests standard [Ref 8].

quiz.text: Which drugs exhibit ZERO-ORDER (saturable / nonlinear) elimination kinetics near therapeutic concentrations, causing small dose increases to produce disproportionate, dangerous spikes in plasma levels?
quiz.stem: Which drugs exhibit ZERO-ORDER (saturable / nonlinear) elimination kinetics near therapeutic concentrations, causing small dose increases to produce disproportionate, dangerous spikes in plasma levels?
options: Phenytoin, Ethanol, and high-dose Salicylates
Penicillin and Gentamicin
Metformin and Lisinopril
Acetaminophen at 500 mg only
hints: In zero-order kinetics, metabolizing enzymes become saturated so a CONSTANT AMOUNT (not constant fraction) is cleared per hour.
Think of the classic 'PEA' mnemonic!
Phenytoin, Ethanol, Aspirin (high-dose) exhibit zero-order saturable elimination [Ch. 71].
quiz.rationale: Phenytoin, ethanol, and high-dose salicylates saturate hepatic metabolizing enzymes near therapeutic levels (zero-order elimination), meaning small dose increments can trigger steep, toxic concentration surges [Ref 30].

quiz.text: How does clinical Decision-Making Capacity differ from legal Competence in Harrison's 22e Ch. 12?
quiz.stem: How does clinical Decision-Making Capacity differ from legal Competence in Harrison's 22e Ch. 12?
options: Only a judge can assess decision-making capacity
Capacity is a clinical, decision-specific judgment made by ANY treating physician at a point in time, whereas competence is a global legal determination made by a court
A diagnosis of schizophrenia automatically eliminates all capacity
Capacity and competence are legally identical
hints: Can a patient have capacity to choose lunch or refuse blood draws while lacking capacity for complex surgery?
Yes! Capacity is task-specific and assessed clinically using the 4 criteria (Understanding, Appreciation, Reasoning, Choice).
Harrison's 22e Ch. 12 clearly separates clinical capacity from judicial competence [Ref 8].
quiz.rationale: Decision-making capacity is evaluated clinically by the treating physician for a specific medical decision at a specific time (and can fluctuate), whereas competence is a formal legal determination by a court [Ref 8].

quiz.text: A hospice patient with end-stage COPD has distressing air hunger despite oxygen and bronchodilators. Which evidence-based palliative intervention from Ch. 13 most effectively relieves refractory dyspnea?
quiz.stem: A hospice patient with end-stage COPD has distressing air hunger despite oxygen and bronchodilators. Which evidence-based palliative intervention from Ch. 13 most effectively relieves refractory dyspnea?
options: Low-dose scheduled/as-needed oral or IV opioids (e.g., morphine) plus a cool handheld fan directed at the face
Routine high-dose IV antibiotics without infection
Withholding all analgesia to avoid slowing respirations
Forced strenuous exercise
hints: Low-dose opioids blunt the brainstem perception of air hunger safely!
A cool fan stimulating trigeminal facial receptors also measurably reduces dyspnea.
Harrison's 22e Ch. 13 designates low-dose opioids as the gold-standard pharmacologic relief for refractory dyspnea [Ref 9].
quiz.rationale: Low-dose opioids directly reduce central respiratory drive mismatch and air hunger, and a cool fan across the face provides adjunctive trigeminal relief in refractory palliative dyspnea [Ref 9].

points.title: High-Yield CYP450 Inducers vs Inhibitors (Bedside Safety Table) [Ref 30]
headers: Clinical Danger When Combined with Narrow-TI Drugs
rows: Rifampin, Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Phenobarbital, St. John's Wort
Treatment failure: Warfarin clot, OCP failure, HIV/transplant rejection
Clarithromycin/Erythromycin, Azole antifungals (Fluconazole/Voriconazole), Ritonavir, Amiodarone, Grapefruit
Life-threatening toxicity: Warfarin hemorrhage, Statin rhabdomyolysis, Digoxin/Tacrolimus toxicity

points.title: Therapeutic Index, Pharmacogenomics & P-Glycoprotein [Ref 30]
points.body: Drugs with a **narrow therapeutic index** (warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, aminoglycosides, tacrolimus, vancomycin) require Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM). **P-glycoprotein (ABCB1)** efflux pumps restrict drug entry across the gut and blood-brain barrier — P-gp inhibitors (verapamil, amiodarone, clarithromycin) can double **digoxin** or **DOAC** levels causing severe toxicity.
